chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Rome. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Flavius, Marullus, and a throng of Citizens.]

FLAVIUS. Get off the streets! Go home, you lazy creatures, go home. Is this a holiday? Don't you know that as working men you shouldn't walk around on a workday without the marks of your trade? Speak up — what's your trade?
CARPENTER. Why, sir, I'm a carpenter.
MARULLUS. Where's your leather apron and your ruler? What are you doing in your best clothes? And you, sir — what's your trade?
COBBLER. Honestly, sir, compared to a fine workman, I'm only what you'd call a cobbler.
MARULLUS. But what trade are you? Answer me straight.
COBBLER. A trade, sir, that I hope I can practice with a clear conscience — I'm a mender of bad soles.
MARULLUS. What trade, you rogue? You bad-mannered rogue, what trade?
COBBLER. No, please, sir, don't lose your temper with me. But if you're out of sorts, sir, I can mend you.
MARULLUS. What do you mean by that? Mend me, you cheeky fellow?
COBBLER. Why, sir, cobble you.
FLAVIUS. So you're a cobbler, are you?

COBBLER. Truly, sir, I make my living with the awl. I don't meddle in any other tradesman's business, nor in women's business — but really, sir, I'm a surgeon to old shoes. When they're in serious trouble, I save them. As fine men as ever walked in leather shoes have walked on my handiwork.
FLAVIUS. But why aren't you in your shop today? Why are you leading these men through the streets?
COBBLER. Truly, sir, to wear out their shoes and get myself more work. But honestly, sir, we're taking a holiday to see Caesar and celebrate his triumph.

MARULLUS. Celebrate what? What victory does he bring home? What conquered kings follow his chariot to Rome in chains? You blockheads, you stones, you things worse than senseless! O you hard hearts, you cruel men of Rome — have you forgotten Pompey? Many and many a time you climbed up to the walls and battlements, to towers and windows, even to the chimney tops, with your babies in your arms, and you sat there all day long, patiently waiting to see great Pompey pass through the streets of Rome. And when his chariot appeared, didn't you raise such a universal shout that the Tiber trembled underneath her banks to hear the echo of your cries from her hollow shores? And now you put on your best clothes? And now you pick out a holiday? And now you scatter flowers in the path of one who rides triumphant over Pompey's blood? Get out of here! Run to your houses, fall on your knees, pray to the gods to hold back the plague that must surely fall on such ingratitude.

FLAVIUS. Go, go, my countrymen, and to make up for this fault, gather all the poor men like yourselves, lead them to the banks of the Tiber, and weep your tears into the channel until even the lowest stream rises to kiss the highest shore.
[Exeunt Citizens.]

See how even the lowest of them is moved — they slip away tongue-tied with guilt. You go down that way toward the Capitol; I'll go this way. Strip the statues if you find them decorated with garlands.
MARULLUS. Can we do that? You know it's the feast of Lupercal.

FLAVIUS. It doesn't matter. Don't let any statues be hung with Caesar's trophies. I'll go and drive the common people off the streets — you do the same wherever you see them crowding. These growing feathers, plucked from Caesar's wing, will keep him flying at an ordinary height. Otherwise he'd soar out of sight of ordinary men and keep us all in servile fear.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. A public place
paragraphs: [Enter, in procession, with music: Caesar; Antony, dressed for the race; Calphurnia, Portia, Decius, Cicero, Brutus, Cassius, and Casca; a great crowd following, among them a Soothsayer.]
CAESAR. Calphurnia.
CASCA. Quiet, everyone — Caesar speaks.
[Music ceases.]
CAESAR. Calphurnia.
CALPHURNIA. Here, my lord.
CAESAR. Stand directly in Antony's path when he runs his course. Antony.
ANTONY. Yes, Caesar?
CAESAR. Don't forget, in your hurry, to touch Calphurnia. Our elders say that childless women, touched during this sacred race, shake off their barrenness.
ANTONY. I'll remember. When Caesar says "Do this," it is done.
CAESAR. Move on, and leave out no ceremony.
[Music.]
SOOTHSAYER. Caesar!
CAESAR. Ha! Who's that calling?
CASCA. Silence every noise. Quiet again!
[Music ceases.]
CAESAR. Who is it in the crowd that's calling me? I hear a voice shriller than all the music crying "Caesar!" Speak — Caesar has turned to listen.
SOOTHSAYER. Beware the Ides of March.
CAESAR. Who's that man?
BRUTUS. A soothsayer telling you to beware the Ides of March.
CAESAR. Bring him in front of me; let me see his face.
CASSIUS. Fellow, come out of the crowd. Look at Caesar.
CAESAR. What do you say to me now? Speak again.
SOOTHSAYER. Beware the Ides of March.
CAESAR. He's a dreamer. Leave him be. Move on.
[Sennet. Exeunt all but Brutus and Cassius.]
CASSIUS. Will you come watch the race?
BRUTUS. Not I.
CASSIUS. Please, do.
BRUTUS. I'm not in the mood for sport. I lack some of the quick spirit Antony has. Don't let me hold back your pleasures, Cassius. I'll leave you.

CASSIUS. Brutus, I've been watching you lately. I no longer see in your eyes the warmth and show of affection you used to have. You're treating a friend who loves you with too cold and distant a hand.

BRUTUS. Cassius, don't be mistaken. If I've hidden my expression, the trouble in my face is turned only against myself. Lately I've been vexed by conflicting passions, thoughts that concern only me, which perhaps stain my behavior. But don't let my good friends — and you, Cassius, are one of them — be grieved by it, or read anything more into my neglect than that poor Brutus, at war with himself, forgets to show love to other men.

CASSIUS. Then, Brutus, I have badly misjudged your feelings, and because of it I've kept buried in my chest thoughts of great value, ideas worth speaking. Tell me, good Brutus — can you see your own face?
BRUTUS. No, Cassius. The eye doesn't see itself except by reflection in something else.

CASSIUS. Exactly. And it's a great pity, Brutus, that you have no such mirrors to turn your hidden worth back into your own eye, so you might see your own shadow. I've heard many of the most respected men in Rome — except immortal Caesar — speak of Brutus and, groaning under this age's yoke, wish that noble Brutus had eyes to see what they see.
BRUTUS. What dangers would you lead me into, Cassius, that you'd have me search inside myself for something that isn't there?

CASSIUS. So, good Brutus, prepare to hear me. And since you know you can't see yourself except by reflection, I, your mirror, will modestly reveal to you that part of yourself which you don't yet know. And don't be suspicious of me, gentle Brutus. If I were a common joker, or used cheap oaths to vow my love to every new flatterer; if you know that I fawn on men, hug them tight, and then slander them behind their backs; or if you know that I bare my soul over drinks to every rabble, then count me dangerous.
[Flourish and shout.]
BRUTUS. What's all that shouting? I'm afraid the people are choosing Caesar for their king.
CASSIUS. Yes — and that troubles you? Then you don't want it to happen.

BRUTUS. I don't, Cassius — though I love him well. But why are you keeping me here so long? What is it you want to share with me? If it's anything for the general good, set honor in one eye and death in the other, and I'll look on both alike. Let the gods help me as I love the name of honor more than I fear death.

CASSIUS. I know that virtue is in you, Brutus, as well as I know your outward face. Well, honor is the subject of my story. I can't tell what you and other men think of this life, but for myself, I'd rather not exist than live in awe of a creature like myself. I was born as free as Caesar; so were you. We've both been fed as well, and we can both endure winter's cold as well as he can. Once, on a raw and gusty day, when the troubled Tiber was chafing against her banks, Caesar said to me, "Do you dare, Cassius, leap into this angry flood with me, and swim to that point over there?" At the word, dressed as I was, I plunged in and told him to follow. He did. The torrent roared, and we beat against it with strong muscles, throwing it aside, stemming it with hearts of competition. But before we could reach the point we'd aimed at, Caesar cried, "Help me, Cassius, or I sink!" Just as Aeneas, our great ancestor, bore old Anchises on his shoulder from the flames of Troy, so I bore tired Caesar from the waves of the Tiber. And this man has now become a god — and Cassius is a wretched creature who must bow his body if Caesar so much as carelessly nods at him. He had a fever when he was in Spain, and when the fit was on him, I noticed how he shook. It's true — this god did shake. His cowardly lips lost their color, and that same eye whose glance overawes the world lost its luster. I heard him groan — yes, and that tongue of his that commanded the Romans to mark his words and write his speeches in their books, alas, it cried, "Give me some drink, Titinius," like a sick girl. Ye gods, it amazes me that a man of such feeble nature should get such a head start on the majestic world and bear the prize alone.
[Shout. Flourish.]
BRUTUS. Another general shout? I believe these cheers are for some new honors being heaped on Caesar.

CASSIUS. Why, man, he bestrides the narrow world like a Colossus, and we petty men walk under his huge legs and peer around to find ourselves dishonorable graves. Men at some point are masters of their own fates. The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars but in ourselves, that we are underlings. "Brutus" and "Caesar" — what's so special in that "Caesar"? Why should that name be sounded louder than yours? Write them together — yours is just as fair a name. Say them aloud — it sits in the mouth just as well. Weigh them — they're equally heavy. Use them to summon spirits — "Brutus" will raise one as quickly as "Caesar." Now, in the name of all the gods at once, what is this Caesar of ours eating that he's grown so great? Age, you should be ashamed! Rome, you've lost the breed of noble bloods! When has there been an age since the great flood that wasn't famed for more than just one man? When could anyone speaking of Rome ever say, until now, that her wide walls contained only one man? Now it really is Rome — there's plenty of room in it, since there's only one man in it. Oh, you and I have heard our fathers say there was once a Brutus who would have endured the everlasting devil ruling Rome as readily as a king.

BRUTUS. I don't doubt that you love me. I have some sense of what you'd push me toward. How I've thought about this, and about these times, I'll tell you another day. For now, by your love, I beg you, urge me no further. What you've said, I'll consider; what you have to say, I'll hear patiently. And I'll find a proper time both to hear and to answer such weighty matters. Till then, my noble friend, chew on this: Brutus would rather be a peasant villager than count himself a son of Rome under the harsh conditions this time is likely to lay on us.
CASSIUS. I'm glad my weak words have struck even this much spark of fire from Brutus.
[Enter Caesar and his train.]
BRUTUS. The games are done, and Caesar is coming back.
CASSIUS. As they pass by, pluck Casca by the sleeve. He'll tell you in his sour way what worth-noting things have happened today.

BRUTUS. I will. But look, Cassius — the angry spot is glowing on Caesar's brow, and all the rest look like a scolded retinue. Calphurnia's cheek is pale, and Cicero is glaring with the same ferret-eyed, fiery look we've seen him wear in the Capitol when he's been crossed in argument by some senators.
CASSIUS. Casca will tell us what the matter is.
CAESAR. Antony.
ANTONY. Caesar?
CAESAR. Let me have men around me who are fat — smooth-headed men, and ones who sleep at night. That Cassius over there has a lean and hungry look. He thinks too much. Such men are dangerous.
ANTONY. Don't fear him, Caesar — he's not dangerous. He's a noble Roman and well-disposed.

CAESAR. I wish he were fatter! But I don't fear him. Still, if my nature were given to fear, I don't know the man I'd avoid sooner than that spare Cassius. He reads a lot, he's a great observer, and he looks right through the deeds of men. He loves no plays, as you do, Antony. He hears no music. He seldom smiles, and when he does, he smiles in such a way that it's as if he mocks himself and scorns his own spirit for being moved to smile at anything. Such men as he are never at heart's ease while they're looking at someone greater than themselves, and that's why they're very dangerous. I'm telling you what is to be feared, not what I fear — for I am always Caesar. Come around to my right side, this ear is deaf, and tell me truly what you think of him.
[Exeunt Caesar and his train. Casca stays.]
CASCA. You tugged on my cloak. Did you want to speak with me?
BRUTUS. Yes, Casca, tell us what happened today that makes Caesar look so grim.
CASCA. Why, you were with him, weren't you?
BRUTUS. I wouldn't be asking Casca what had happened if I were.
CASCA. Well, a crown was offered to him, and when it was offered, he pushed it away with the back of his hand, like this; and then the people started shouting.
BRUTUS. What was the second shout for?
CASCA. Why, the same thing.
CASSIUS. They shouted three times. What was the last cry for?
CASCA. The same thing again.
BRUTUS. Was the crown offered to him three times?
CASCA. Yes, indeed, three times — and he pushed it away three times, each time more gently than the last, and every time he pushed it away my honest neighbors shouted.
CASSIUS. Who offered him the crown?
CASCA. Why, Antony.
BRUTUS. Tell us how it happened, gentle Casca.

CASCA. I'd as soon be hanged as try to tell how it happened — it was sheer foolery, I didn't pay it much attention. I saw Mark Antony offer him a crown — and yet it wasn't really a crown, it was one of those coronets — and as I told you, he pushed it away once. But, all the same, to my thinking, he would gladly have taken it. Then Antony offered it again. He pushed it away again. But to my thinking, he was very reluctant to take his fingers off it. And then Antony offered it a third time. He pushed it away the third time. And every time he refused it, the rabble hooted and clapped their chapped hands and threw up their sweaty nightcaps, and let out such a stink of foul breath because Caesar refused the crown that it almost choked Caesar — for he fainted and fell down at it. As for me, I didn't dare laugh, for fear of opening my lips and breathing in the bad air.
CASSIUS. But wait — please. Did Caesar actually faint?
CASCA. He fell down in the marketplace, foamed at the mouth, and was speechless.
BRUTUS. That's likely enough — he has epilepsy.
CASSIUS. No, Caesar doesn't have it. But you and I and honest Casca — we have the falling sickness.

CASCA. I don't know what you mean by that, but I'm sure Caesar fell down. If the rag-tag people didn't cheer him and hiss him according to whether he pleased or displeased them — as they do the actors in the theater — then I'm no honest man.
BRUTUS. What did he say when he came to?

CASCA. Well, before he fell, when he saw the common herd was glad he refused the crown, he pulled open his doublet and offered them his throat to cut. If I'd been a workingman, I'd have taken him at his word, or may I go to hell among the rogues. And so he fell. When he came to himself again, he said that if he had done or said anything wrong, he hoped their worships would put it down to his illness. Three or four wenches where I stood cried, "Alas, good soul!" and forgave him with all their hearts. But there's no notice to be taken of them — if Caesar had stabbed their mothers, they'd have done the same.
BRUTUS. And after that, he came away looking so grim?
CASCA. Yes.
CASSIUS. Did Cicero say anything?
CASCA. Yes — he spoke in Greek.
CASSIUS. To what effect?

CASCA. Well, if I tell you that, I'll never look you in the face again. But those who understood him smiled at one another and shook their heads — but for my own part, it was Greek to me. I could tell you more news, too: Marullus and Flavius, for pulling scarves off Caesar's statues, have been silenced. Farewell. There was more foolery yet, if I could remember it.
CASSIUS. Will you have supper with me tonight, Casca?
CASCA. No, I'm promised elsewhere.
CASSIUS. Will you dine with me tomorrow?
CASCA. Yes, if I'm alive, and your mind hasn't changed, and your dinner is worth eating.
CASSIUS. Good. I'll expect you.
CASCA. Do so. Farewell, both of you.
[Exit Casca.]
BRUTUS. What a blunt fellow he's become! He was quick-witted in his school days.

CASSIUS. He still is, in carrying out any bold or noble enterprise — however much he puts on this slow manner. This rudeness is a sauce to his good wit, which makes men's appetites readier to digest his words.
BRUTUS. So it is. For now I'll leave you. Tomorrow, if you want to speak with me, I'll come to your house; or, if you prefer, come to mine, and I'll wait for you.
CASSIUS. I'll do so. Till then, think on the state of the world.
[Exit Brutus.]

Well, Brutus, you are noble. Yet I see that your honorable mettle can be worked away from what it's naturally disposed toward. So it's only fitting that noble minds keep company with their own kind, for who is so firm he can't be seduced? Caesar bears me a grudge, but he loves Brutus. If I were Brutus now, and he were Cassius, he wouldn't manipulate me. Tonight, in several different handwritings, I'll throw in at his windows, as if they came from several citizens, writings all pointing to the great opinion Rome holds of his name — in which Caesar's ambition will be hinted at obliquely. And after this, let Caesar sit his throne secure, for we will shake him — or endure worse days.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — The same. A street
paragraphs: [Thunder and lightning. Enter, from opposite sides, Casca with his sword drawn, and Cicero.]
CICERO. Good evening, Casca. Did you escort Caesar home? Why are you breathless, and why are you staring like that?

CASCA. Aren't you shaken when the whole frame of the earth shakes like something unsteady? O Cicero, I've seen storms when the howling winds split the knotty oaks; I've seen the ambitious ocean swell and rage and foam, lifted to meet the threatening clouds. But never until tonight, never until now, did I walk through a storm that dropped fire. Either there's civil war in heaven, or else the world has insulted the gods so far that they're sending destruction.
CICERO. Why, did you see anything else remarkable?

CASCA. A common slave — you'd know him well by sight — held up his left hand, which flamed and burned like twenty torches together, and yet his hand, feeling no fire, was not scorched. Besides — I haven't sheathed my sword since — by the Capitol I met a lion that glared at me and went sullenly by without harming me. And there was a heap of a hundred terrified women, transformed by their fear, who swore they had seen men, all on fire, walking up and down the streets. And yesterday the night-owl sat at noon in the marketplace, hooting and shrieking. When such omens come together, don't let men say, "They have natural causes; this is nothing." I believe these are warning signs to the country they point toward.
CICERO. Indeed, it's a strange-tempered time. But men can interpret things to suit themselves, completely missing the actual meaning of the things. Is Caesar coming to the Capitol tomorrow?
CASCA. He is — he told Antony to send word to you that he'd be there tomorrow.
CICERO. Goodnight then, Casca. This troubled sky is no weather to walk in.
CASCA. Farewell, Cicero.
[Exit Cicero.]
[Enter Cassius.]
CASSIUS. Who's there?
CASCA. A Roman.
CASSIUS. Casca — by your voice.
CASCA. Your ear is sharp. Cassius, what a night this is!
CASSIUS. A very pleasing night to honest men.
CASCA. Who has ever known the heavens to threaten like this?

CASSIUS. Those who have known the earth to be so full of faults. As for me, I've walked through the streets giving myself up to the dangerous night; and unbuttoned like this, Casca, as you see, I've bared my chest to the thunderbolts. And when the jagged blue lightning seemed to split open the breast of heaven, I stood directly in its target and flash.
CASCA. But why did you tempt the heavens so? It's a man's part to fear and tremble when the mightiest gods send such dreadful heralds to astonish us.

CASSIUS. You're dull, Casca. The sparks of life that should be in a Roman are missing in you — or else you don't use them. You look pale, you stare, you take on fear and amazement at the strange impatience of the heavens. But if you considered the true cause why all these fires burn, why all these ghosts glide by, why birds and beasts deviate from their nature and kind, why old men, fools, and children prophesy, why all these things change from their normal order and their pre-formed natures into monstrous behavior — why, you'd find that heaven has filled them with these spirits to make them instruments of fear and warning toward some monstrous condition of the state. Now I could, Casca, name to you a man most like this dreadful night — a man who thunders, lightens, opens graves, and roars like the lion in the Capitol; a man no mightier than yourself or me in personal action, yet grown to monstrous size and as fearsome as these strange disturbances are.
CASCA. It's Caesar you mean, isn't it, Cassius?

CASSIUS. Whoever it is. Romans today still have the muscles and limbs of their ancestors, but — alas! — our fathers' minds are dead, and we're ruled by our mothers' spirits. Our yoke and our submission to it show us to be womanish.
CASCA. Indeed, they say the senators tomorrow plan to make Caesar a king, and he'll wear his crown by sea and land in every place except here in Italy.

CASSIUS. Then I know where I'll wear this dagger. Cassius will free Cassius from bondage. In this, you gods, you make the weak strongest; in this, you gods, you defeat tyrants. No stone tower, no walls of beaten brass, no airless dungeon, no strong iron chains can hold back the strength of the spirit. Life, when it's tired of these worldly bars, always has the power to dismiss itself. If I know this, let all the world know besides — the part of tyranny that I bear, I can throw off when I please.
[Thunder continues.]
CASCA. So can I. Every slave holds in his own hand the power to cancel his captivity.

CASSIUS. And why should Caesar be a tyrant then? Poor man — I know he wouldn't be a wolf if he didn't see that the Romans are only sheep. He wouldn't be a lion if Romans weren't deer. Those who'd quickly make a mighty fire begin it with weak straws. What trash Rome is, what rubbish, what offal, when it serves only as kindling to set ablaze so vile a thing as Caesar! But, oh grief, where have you led me? I'm perhaps saying this in front of a willing slave. In that case I know I'll have to answer for it — but I'm armed, and dangers are indifferent to me.

CASCA. You're speaking to Casca, and to a man who is no sneering tell-tale. Take my hand. Form a faction to put right all these wrongs, and I'll set my foot as far forward as anyone who goes farthest.

CASSIUS. There's a bargain made. Now know this, Casca — I've already moved several of the noblest-minded Romans to undertake with me a venture of honorable and dangerous consequence. I know by now that they're waiting for me at Pompey's Porch — for tonight, this fearful night, there's no stir or movement in the streets; and the look of the elements above matches the work we have in hand: most bloody, fiery, and most terrible.
[Enter Cinna.]
CASCA. Stay back a moment — someone's coming in a hurry.
CASSIUS. It's Cinna — I know him by his walk. He's a friend. Cinna, where are you hurrying to?
CINNA. To find you. Who's that? Metellus Cimber?
CASSIUS. No, it's Casca — a man now joined to our undertaking. Aren't they waiting for me, Cinna?
CINNA. I'm glad of that. What a fearful night this is! Two or three of us have seen strange sights.
CASSIUS. Aren't they waiting for me? Tell me.
CINNA. Yes, they are. O Cassius, if you could only win noble Brutus to our side—

CASSIUS. Be content. Good Cinna, take this paper and lay it in the praetor's chair where Brutus is sure to find it. Throw this in at his window. Set this up with wax on old Brutus's statue. When you've done all that, head to Pompey's Porch, where you'll find us. Are Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?
CINNA. All but Metellus Cimber — he's gone to look for you at your house. Well, I'll hurry, and place these papers as you've told me.
CASSIUS. When you're done, head to Pompey's theatre.
[Exit Cinna.]
Come, Casca, you and I will yet, before daylight, see Brutus at his house. Three parts of him are ours already, and at our next meeting the whole man will yield to us.
CASCA. Oh, he sits high in all the people's hearts! What would look like a crime if we did it, his backing — like the richest alchemy — will transform into virtue and worthiness.
CASSIUS. You've grasped him, and his worth, and our great need of him exactly right. Let's go — it's after midnight, and before daylight we'll wake him and make sure of him.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Rome. Brutus’ orchard
paragraphs: [Enter Brutus.]
BRUTUS. Hey, Lucius! I can't tell from the stars how close to daybreak it is. Lucius, I say! I wish my fault were that I slept so soundly. When, Lucius, when? Wake up, I say! Hey, Lucius!
[Enter Lucius.]
LUCIUS. Did you call, my lord?
BRUTUS. Get me a candle in my study, Lucius. When it's lit, come and call me here.
LUCIUS. I will, my lord.
[Exit.]

BRUTUS. It has to be by his death. And for myself, I have no personal cause to attack him — only the general one. He wants to be crowned. How that might change his nature — that's the question. It's the bright day that brings out the adder, and that calls for wary walking. Crown him? Yes — and then, I admit, we put a sting in him that he can use to do harm at will. The abuse of greatness comes when it cuts conscience away from power. And to speak truly of Caesar, I've never known a time when his feelings ruled him more than his reason. But it's a familiar truth that humility is young ambition's ladder, which the climber faces as he goes up. But once he reaches the topmost rung, he turns his back on the ladder, looks toward the clouds, and scorns the lower steps by which he ascended. So Caesar may do. Then, in case he might, prevent it. And since the quarrel can't be justified by what he is right now, frame it like this: that what he is, magnified, would run to such-and-such extremes. So think of him as a serpent's egg — which, once hatched, would, like its kind, grow dangerous — and kill him in the shell.
[Enter Lucius.]
LUCIUS. The candle is burning in your study, sir. Searching the window for a flint, I found this paper, sealed up like this, and I'm sure it wasn't lying there when I went to bed.
[Gives him the letter.]
BRUTUS. Go back to bed. It's not day yet. Isn't tomorrow, boy, the Ides of March?
LUCIUS. I don't know, sir.
BRUTUS. Look at the calendar and let me know.
LUCIUS. I will, sir.
[Exit.]
BRUTUS. The meteors flashing through the air give off enough light that I can read by them.
[Opens the letter and reads.]

"Brutus, you sleep. Awake and look at yourself. Shall Rome, etc. Speak, strike, redress!" "Brutus, you sleep. Awake!" Such hints have often been dropped where I have picked them up. "Shall Rome, etc." I must fill it in like this: Shall Rome stand under one man's domination? What, Rome? My ancestors drove the Tarquin from the streets of Rome when he was called a king. "Speak, strike, redress!" Am I being asked to speak and strike? O Rome, I promise you: if redress follows, you'll receive your full petition at the hand of Brutus.
[Enter Lucius.]
LUCIUS. Sir, fifteen days of March are gone.
[Knock within.]
BRUTUS. Good. Go to the gate — somebody's knocking.
[Exit Lucius.]

Since Cassius first sharpened me against Caesar, I haven't slept. Between the doing of a dreadful thing and the first impulse to do it, all the interval is like a hallucination or a hideous dream. The mind and the body, its instrument, are then in council, and the state of a man, like a little kingdom, suffers something like an insurrection.
[Enter Lucius.]
LUCIUS. Sir, it's your brother Cassius at the door, who wants to see you.
BRUTUS. Is he alone?
LUCIUS. No, sir. There are more with him.
BRUTUS. Do you know them?
LUCIUS. No, sir, their hats are pulled down over their ears and half their faces are hidden in their cloaks, so there's no way for me to recognize them by any feature.
BRUTUS. Let them in.
[Exit Lucius.]

It's the faction. O conspiracy, are you ashamed to show your dangerous face by night, when evils are most free? Then, by day, where will you find a cave dark enough to mask your monstrous face? Don't bother looking, conspiracy — hide it in smiles and friendliness. For if you walked with your true face on, not Erebus itself would be dim enough to hide you from being stopped.
[Enter Cassius, Casca, Decius, Cinna, Metellus Cimber, and Trebonius.]
CASSIUS. I think we're imposing too much on your rest. Good morning, Brutus. Are we troubling you?
BRUTUS. I've been up an hour — awake all night. Do I know these men who've come with you?
CASSIUS. Yes, every one of them — and no man here who doesn't honor you, and everyone wishes you held the same opinion of yourself that every noble Roman holds of you. This is Trebonius.
BRUTUS. He's welcome here.
CASSIUS. This is Decius Brutus.
BRUTUS. He's welcome too.
CASSIUS. This is Casca; this is Cinna; and this is Metellus Cimber.
BRUTUS. All welcome. What watchful cares come between your eyes and sleep?
CASSIUS. May I have a word?
[They whisper.]
DECIUS. Here's the east. Doesn't the day break here?
CASCA. No.
CINNA. Oh, pardon me, sir, it does — and those grey streaks fretting the clouds are heralds of day.

CASCA. You'll both admit you're mistaken. Here, where I point my sword, the sun rises — which, considering the youthful season of the year, is a long way south. Two months from now, higher toward the north, it first shows its fire; and the true east stands, as the Capitol does, directly here.
BRUTUS. Give me all your hands, one by one.
CASSIUS. And let us swear our resolve.

BRUTUS. No, not an oath. If the faces of men, the suffering of our souls, the abuse of these times — if these aren't motive enough, break off in time, and every man home to his idle bed. So let high-aimed tyranny range on, until every man falls by lottery. But if these things — and I'm sure they do — bear fire enough to kindle cowards, and to steel the melting spirits of women with valor, then, countrymen, what spur do we need beyond our own cause to prick us to action? What other bond than secret Romans who have spoken the word and won't equivocate? And what other oath than honesty pledged to honesty, that this shall be done or we'll fall trying? Let priests swear, and cowards, and cautious men, old feeble carcasses, and the kind of suffering souls who welcome wrongs. Let creatures men distrust swear to bad causes. But don't stain the even virtue of our enterprise, nor the unsuppressible mettle of our spirits, by thinking that either our cause or our performance needs an oath — when every drop of blood that every Roman bears, and nobly bears, is guilty of a kind of bastardy if he breaks the smallest part of any promise he's made.
CASSIUS. But what about Cicero? Shall we sound him out? I think he'll stand very strongly with us.
CASCA. Let's not leave him out.
CINNA. No, by no means.

METELLUS. Oh, let's have him — his silver hair will buy us a good reputation and win men's voices to praise our deeds. It will be said his judgment guided our hands. Our youth and our wildness won't show at all — it will all be hidden by his gravity.
BRUTUS. Oh, don't name him. Let's not share this with him — he'll never follow anything that other men begin.
CASSIUS. Then leave him out.
CASCA. He's not the right fit.
DECIUS. Is no one else to be touched — only Caesar?

CASSIUS. Decius, good point. I don't think it's wise that Mark Antony, so well-loved by Caesar, should outlive Caesar. We'll find him a shrewd schemer; and you know his means, if he uses them, could stretch far enough to trouble us all. To prevent that, let Antony and Caesar fall together.

BRUTUS. Our course will look too bloody, Caius Cassius, if we cut the head off and then hack the limbs — like wrath in death and envy after. Antony is only a limb of Caesar. Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius. We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar, and in the spirit of men there's no blood. Oh, if only we could come at Caesar's spirit without dismembering Caesar! But, alas, Caesar must bleed for it. And, gentle friends, let's kill him boldly, but not wrathfully. Let's carve him as a dish fit for the gods, not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds. And let our hearts, like subtle masters, stir up their servants to an act of rage, and afterward seem to chide them. This will mark our purpose as necessary, not envious. So appearing to the common eye, we'll be called purgers, not murderers. And as for Mark Antony — don't think of him. He can do no more than Caesar's arm once Caesar's head is off.
CASSIUS. Still, I fear him — for the deep-rooted love he bears to Caesar—

BRUTUS. No, good Cassius, don't think of him. If he loves Caesar, all he can do is to himself — go into mourning and die for Caesar. And that would be much for him to do, since he's given to sports, to wildness, and to plenty of company.
TREBONIUS. There's nothing to fear in him. Don't let him die — he'll live and laugh at this later.
[Clock strikes.]
BRUTUS. Quiet! Count the hour.
CASSIUS. The clock has struck three.
TREBONIUS. It's time to part.

CASSIUS. But it's still uncertain whether Caesar will come out today or not. He's grown superstitious lately, quite contrary to the firm opinion he once held against fantasy, dreams, and ceremonies. It may be these obvious omens, the unaccustomed terror of this night, and the urging of his augurers may keep him from the Capitol today.

DECIUS. Never fear that. If he's that resolved, I can sway him — he loves to hear that unicorns may be trapped with trees, bears with mirrors, elephants with pitfalls, lions with snares, and men with flatterers. But when I tell him he hates flatterers, he says he does — being then most flattered of all. Let me work on him — I can give his mood the right turn, and I'll bring him to the Capitol.
CASSIUS. No, we'll all go and fetch him.
BRUTUS. By eight o'clock. Is that the latest?
CINNA. Let that be the latest, and don't fail then.
METELLUS. Caius Ligarius has a grudge against Caesar, who reprimanded him for speaking well of Pompey. I'm surprised none of you have thought of him.
BRUTUS. Now, good Metellus, go by his house. He loves me well, and I've given him reason to. Just send him here, and I'll shape him.
CASSIUS. Morning's coming. We'll leave you, Brutus. And, friends, disperse — but all of you remember what you've said, and show yourselves true Romans.
BRUTUS. Good gentlemen, look fresh and cheerful. Don't let our faces wear our purposes; carry it as our Roman actors do, with tireless spirits and a formal composure. And so, good morning to you all.
[Exeunt all but Brutus.]

Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? No matter — enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber. You have no figures or fantasies in your head that busy care draws in the brains of men, and that's why you sleep so soundly.
[Enter Portia.]
PORTIA. Brutus, my lord.
BRUTUS. Portia, what do you mean? Why are you up now? It isn't good for your health to commit your delicate condition to the raw cold morning.

PORTIA. Nor for yours either. You stole ungently from my bed, Brutus. And yesterday at supper you suddenly got up and walked about, brooding and sighing, with your arms folded. When I asked you what was wrong, you stared at me with ungentle looks. I pressed you further; then you scratched your head and stamped your foot too impatiently. Still I insisted; still you wouldn't answer. With an angry wave of your hand you signaled me to leave you. So I did, afraid to deepen the impatience that seemed too much kindled — and hoping it was only an effect of mood, which sometimes has its hour with every man. It won't let you eat, or talk, or sleep; and if it could work as much on your appearance as it has on your behavior, I wouldn't recognize you, Brutus. Dear my lord, let me share the cause of your grief.
BRUTUS. I'm not well in health, that's all.
PORTIA. Brutus is wise — and if he weren't well, he'd take the means to become so.
BRUTUS. Why, that's what I'm doing. Good Portia, go to bed.

PORTIA. Is Brutus sick? And is it medicinal to walk about unbuttoned and breathe in the vapors of the dank morning? What — is Brutus sick, and will he steal out of his wholesome bed to dare the vile contagion of the night, and tempt the rheumy, foul air to add to his sickness? No, my Brutus — you have some sick offense in your mind, which, by the right and virtue of my place, I ought to know about. And on my knees, I conjure you, by my once-praised beauty, by all your vows of love, and by the great vow that incorporated us and made us one — unfold to me, your self, your half, why you are heavy, and what men have come to you tonight. For there have been some six or seven who hid their faces even from the darkness.
BRUTUS. Don't kneel, gentle Portia.

PORTIA. I shouldn't need to, if you were gentle Brutus. Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus — is it stipulated that I should know no secrets that belong to you? Am I your self only in a limited, partial way — to keep with you at meals, to comfort your bed, to talk with you sometimes? Do I live only in the suburbs of your good pleasure? If that's all, Portia is Brutus's whore, not his wife.
BRUTUS. You are my true and honorable wife, as dear to me as the ruddy drops that visit my sad heart.

PORTIA. If that were true, then I would know this secret. I admit I'm a woman — but a woman that Lord Brutus took to wife. I admit I'm a woman — but a woman of good reputation, Cato's daughter. Do you think I'm no stronger than my sex, having such a father and such a husband? Tell me your counsels — I won't disclose them. I've given strong proof of my constancy — giving myself a voluntary wound, here, in the thigh. Can I bear that patiently, and not my husband's secrets?
BRUTUS. O you gods, make me worthy of this noble wife!
[Knock.]

Listen, listen — someone's knocking. Portia, go in for a while; soon your bosom shall share the secrets of my heart. All my engagements I'll explain to you, all the markings on my sad brow. Leave me quickly.
[Exit Portia.]
[Enter Lucius with Ligarius.]
Lucius, who's knocking?
LUCIUS. Here's a sick man who wants to speak with you.
BRUTUS. Caius Ligarius, the one Metellus mentioned. Boy, stand aside. Caius Ligarius — how are you?
LIGARIUS. Accept a good-morning from a feeble tongue.
BRUTUS. Oh, what a time you've picked, brave Caius, to be wearing a sick man's headcloth! I wish you weren't sick.
LIGARIUS. I'm not sick, if Brutus has in hand any exploit worthy of the name of honor.
BRUTUS. Such an exploit I do have in hand, Ligarius, if you had a healthy ear to hear of it.

LIGARIUS. By all the gods Romans bow before, I throw off my sickness here and now. Soul of Rome! Brave son, descended from honorable loins! You, like an exorcist, have conjured up my mortified spirit. Now bid me run, and I'll struggle with impossibilities — yes, get the better of them. What's to do?
BRUTUS. A piece of work that will make sick men whole.
LIGARIUS. But aren't there some well men we must make sick?
BRUTUS. That, too. What it is, my Caius, I'll unfold to you as we're going, to the one it must be done to.
LIGARIUS. Lead the way, and with a heart newly fired I'll follow you, to do I know not what — but it's enough that Brutus leads me on.
[Thunder.]
BRUTUS. Follow me then.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — A room in Caesar’s palace
paragraphs: [Thunder and lightning. Enter Caesar, in his nightgown.]
CAESAR. Neither heaven nor earth has been at peace tonight. Three times in her sleep Calphurnia cried out, "Help! They murder Caesar!" Who's there?
[Enter a Servant.]
SERVANT. My lord?
CAESAR. Go tell the priests to perform a sacrifice now, and bring me back their reading of the outcome.
SERVANT. I will, my lord.
[Exit.]
[Enter Calphurnia.]
CALPHURNIA. What are you thinking of, Caesar? Are you going out? You shall not leave the house today.
CAESAR. Caesar shall go out. The things that have threatened me have only looked on my back. Once they see the face of Caesar, they vanish.

CALPHURNIA. Caesar, I've never made much of omens, but now they frighten me. There's a man inside, in addition to what we've heard and seen ourselves, who's telling of the most horrible sights seen by the watch. A lioness has given birth in the streets, graves have yawned open and yielded up their dead. Fierce, fiery warriors fight in the clouds in ranks and squadrons and proper formations of war, raining blood on the Capitol. The noise of battle clashed in the air, horses neighed, dying men groaned, and ghosts shrieked and squealed through the streets. O Caesar, these things are beyond all natural order, and I fear them.
CAESAR. What can be avoided whose end is determined by the mighty gods? Yet Caesar shall go out. These predictions apply to the world in general as much as to Caesar.
CALPHURNIA. When beggars die, no comets are seen. The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.

CAESAR. Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once. Of all the wonders I've yet heard, it seems to me strangest that men should fear, seeing that death, a necessary end, will come when it will come.
[Enter Servant.]
What do the augurers say?
SERVANT. They wouldn't have you go out today. Drawing the entrails from an offering, they could not find a heart inside the beast.

CAESAR. The gods do this to shame cowardice. Caesar would be a beast without a heart if he stayed at home today out of fear. No, Caesar shall not. Danger knows full well that Caesar is more dangerous than he is. We are two lions born of one litter on the same day, and I the elder and more terrible — and Caesar shall go out.

CALPHURNIA. Alas, my lord, your wisdom is consumed by your confidence. Don't go out today. Call it my fear that keeps you in the house, not your own. We'll send Mark Antony to the Senate-house, and he shall say you're not well today. Let me, on my knee, prevail in this.
CAESAR. Mark Antony shall say I'm not well, and to humor you I'll stay at home.
[Enter Decius.]
Here's Decius Brutus — he shall tell them so.
DECIUS. Caesar, all hail! Good morning, worthy Caesar. I've come to fetch you to the Senate-house.

CAESAR. And you've come at a very good time to carry my greeting to the senators and tell them I won't come today. To say cannot would be false; to say dare not, even falser. I will not come today. Tell them so, Decius.
CALPHURNIA. Say he's sick.
CAESAR. Shall Caesar send a lie? Have I stretched my arm so far in conquest only to be afraid to tell grey-bearded senators the truth? Decius, go tell them Caesar will not come.
DECIUS. Most mighty Caesar, give me some reason, in case I'm laughed at when I tell them so.

CAESAR. The reason is in my will — I will not come. That is enough to satisfy the Senate. But for your private satisfaction, because I love you, I'll let you know. Calphurnia, my wife, here, is keeping me at home. She dreamt last night that she saw my statue, which, like a fountain with a hundred spouts, ran pure blood — and many lusty Romans came smiling and bathed their hands in it. And these she takes as warnings and omens and imminent evils, and on her knee has begged me to stay at home today.

DECIUS. This dream is entirely misinterpreted. It was a vision fair and fortunate. Your statue spouting blood in many pipes, with so many smiling Romans bathing in it, signifies that from you great Rome shall draw reviving blood, and that great men shall press in for tinctures, stains, relics, and tokens of remembrance. This is what Calphurnia's dream signifies.
CAESAR. And this way you've expounded it well.

DECIUS. I have — when you've heard what I have left to say, and know it now: the Senate has decided to crown mighty Caesar today. If you send word you won't come, their minds may change. Besides, it would be an easy mockery for someone to say, "Break up the Senate till another time, when Caesar's wife has better dreams." If Caesar hides himself, won't they whisper, "Look, Caesar is afraid"? Pardon me, Caesar — my deep, dear love for your career compels me to tell you this; and reason yields to my love.
CAESAR. How foolish your fears seem now, Calphurnia! I'm ashamed I yielded to them. Give me my robe, for I will go.
[Enter Brutus, Ligarius, Metellus, Casca, Trebonius, Cinna, and Publius.]
And look — Publius has come to fetch me.
PUBLIUS. Good morning, Caesar.
CAESAR. Welcome, Publius. What, Brutus, are you up so early too? Good morning, Casca. Caius Ligarius, Caesar was never as much your enemy as that fever that has made you lean. What time is it?
BRUTUS. Caesar, it has just struck eight.
CAESAR. I thank you for your trouble and courtesy.
[Enter Antony.]
See! Antony, who carouses long into the night, is up nonetheless. Good morning, Antony.
ANTONY. The same to most noble Caesar.

CAESAR. Tell them to prepare inside. I'm to blame for being waited on like this. Now, Cinna; now, Metellus; what, Trebonius! I have an hour's worth of talk in store for you. Remember to call on me today. Stay near me, so I don't forget you.
TREBONIUS. Caesar, I will. [Aside.] And so near I will be that your best friends will wish I had been further.
CAESAR. Good friends, go in and taste some wine with me, and then we, like friends, will go together at once.
BRUTUS.
[Aside.] That every like is not the same, O Caesar,
the heart of Brutus aches to think on.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — A street near the Capitol
paragraphs: [Enter Artemidorus, reading a paper.]

ARTEMIDORUS. "Caesar, beware of Brutus; take heed of Cassius; come not near Casca; keep an eye on Cinna; do not trust Trebonius; watch Metellus Cimber closely; Decius Brutus does not love you; you have wronged Caius Ligarius. There is one mind in all these men, and it is set against Caesar. If you are not immortal, look about you: a sense of safety opens the way to conspiracy. The mighty gods defend you! Your friend, Artemidorus." Here I'll stand till Caesar passes by, and as a petitioner I'll give him this. My heart grieves that virtue cannot live out of reach of envy. If you read this, O Caesar, you may live; if not, the Fates conspire with traitors.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — Another part of the same street, before the house of Brutus
paragraphs: [Enter Portia and Lucius.]
PORTIA. Please, boy, run to the Senate-house. Don't stop to answer me — just go. Why are you waiting?
LUCIUS. To know my errand, madam.
PORTIA. I'd want you there and back again before I could tell you what to do there.
[Aside.] O constancy, be strong on my side,
set a huge mountain between my heart and my tongue! I have a man's mind, but a woman's strength. How hard it is for women to keep a secret! Are you still here?
LUCIUS. Madam, what should I do? Run to the Capitol — and nothing else? And then come back to you — and nothing else?

PORTIA. Yes — and bring me word, boy, whether your lord looks well, for he went out looking sickly. And take careful note of what Caesar does, and what petitioners press in around him. Listen, boy — what's that noise?
LUCIUS. I don't hear any, madam.
PORTIA. Please, listen carefully. I heard a bustling murmur, like a brawl, and the wind is carrying it from the Capitol.
LUCIUS. Truly, madam, I hear nothing.
[Enter the Soothsayer.]
PORTIA. Come here, fellow. Where have you been?
SOOTHSAYER. At my own house, good lady.
PORTIA. What time is it?
SOOTHSAYER. About the ninth hour, lady.
PORTIA. Has Caesar gone to the Capitol yet?
SOOTHSAYER. Madam, not yet. I'm going to take up my position to see him pass on his way to the Capitol.
PORTIA. You have some petition for Caesar, don't you?
SOOTHSAYER. That I do, lady. If it will please Caesar to be so good to Caesar as to hear me, I'll beg him to befriend himself.
PORTIA. Why? Do you know of some harm intended toward him?

SOOTHSAYER. None that I know will happen — much that I fear may happen. Good morning to you. The street is narrow here. The crowd that follows Caesar at his heels — senators, praetors, common petitioners — would crush a feeble man almost to death. I'll find a more open spot and speak to great Caesar there as he passes by.
[Exit.]
PORTIA. I must go in.
[Aside.] Ah me, how weak a thing

the heart of a woman is! O Brutus, may the heavens speed your enterprise! Surely the boy heard me. Brutus has a petition Caesar will not grant. Oh, I'm growing faint. Run, Lucius, and give my regards to my lord. Say I am cheerful. Come back to me again, and bring me word what he says to you.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Rome. Before the Capitol; the Senate sitting
paragraphs: [A crowd of people in the street leading to the Capitol. Flourish. Enter Caesar, Brutus, Cassius, Casca, Decius, Metellus, Trebonius, Cinna, Antony, Lepidus, Artemidorus, Publius, Popilius, and the Soothsayer.]
CAESAR. The Ides of March have come.
SOOTHSAYER. Yes, Caesar — but not gone.
ARTEMIDORUS. Hail, Caesar! Read this paper.
DECIUS. Trebonius asks you to look over, at your earliest convenience, this his humble petition.
ARTEMIDORUS. O Caesar, read mine first — mine is a petition that concerns Caesar more closely. Read it, great Caesar.
CAESAR. What concerns me personally shall be served last.
ARTEMIDORUS. Don't delay, Caesar — read it now.
CAESAR. What, is the fellow mad?
PUBLIUS. You there — make way.
CASSIUS. What — are you urging your petitions in the street? Come to the Capitol.
[Caesar enters the Capitol, the rest following. All the Senators rise.]
POPILIUS. I hope your enterprise today may thrive.
CASSIUS. What enterprise, Popilius?
POPILIUS. Fare you well.
[Advances to Caesar.]
BRUTUS. What did Popilius Lena say?
CASSIUS. He wished our enterprise might thrive today. I fear our plan is discovered.
BRUTUS. Look how he's moving toward Caesar — watch him.
CASSIUS. Casca, be quick — we fear we'll be stopped. Brutus, what shall be done? If this is known, either Cassius or Caesar will never go back from this place, for I will kill myself.
BRUTUS. Cassius, stay steady. Popilius Lena isn't talking about our plan — look, he's smiling, and Caesar's expression hasn't changed.
CASSIUS. Trebonius knows his timing — look, Brutus, he's drawing Mark Antony out of the way.
[Exeunt Antony and Trebonius. Caesar and the Senators take their seats.]
DECIUS. Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go and present his petition to Caesar right now.
BRUTUS. He's ready. Press near and second him.
CINNA. Casca, you're the first to raise your hand.
CAESAR. Are we all ready? What is now amiss that Caesar and his Senate must address?
METELLUS. Most high, most mighty, and most powerful Caesar, Metellus Cimber lays before your seat a humble heart.
[Kneeling.]

CAESAR. I must stop you here, Cimber. These crouchings and these grovelling courtesies might fire the blood of ordinary men, and turn established ordinance and original decree into the law of children. Don't be foolish enough to think Caesar carries such rebel blood as can be thawed out of its true quality by what melts fools — I mean sweet words, low bowing curtsies, and base spaniel fawning. Your brother is banished by decree. If you bend and pray and fawn for him, I kick you out of my way like a cur. Know this: Caesar does no wrong, nor will he be satisfied without due cause.
METELLUS. Is there no voice more worthy than my own, to sound more sweetly in great Caesar's ear, to revoke my banished brother's sentence?
BRUTUS. I kiss your hand, but not in flattery, Caesar — asking you that Publius Cimber may have his banishment immediately revoked.
CAESAR. What, Brutus?
CASSIUS. Pardon, Caesar; Caesar, pardon. As low as your foot Cassius falls, to beg the freedom of Publius Cimber.

CAESAR. I could be moved, if I were like you. If I could pray to be moved, prayers would move me. But I am constant as the northern star, of whose true-fixed and resting quality there is no equal in the firmament. The skies are painted with countless sparks; they are all fire, and every one of them shines — but there's only one of them all that holds its place. So in the world: it's well furnished with men, and men are flesh and blood and apprehensive — yet in their number I know only one who, unassailable, holds on to his rank, unshaken by motion. And to show in even a small way that I am he, let me show it in this: that I was constant Cimber should be banished, and I remain constant to keep him so.
CINNA. O Caesar—
CAESAR. Away! Would you try to lift up Mount Olympus?
DECIUS. Great Caesar—
CAESAR. Doesn't Brutus kneel in vain?
CASCA. Speak, hands, for me!
[Casca stabs Caesar in the neck. Caesar catches hold of his arm. He is then stabbed by several other Conspirators, and at last by Marcus Brutus.]
CAESAR. Et tu, Brute? — Then fall, Caesar!
[Dies. The Senators and people retire in confusion.]
CINNA. Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead! Run, proclaim it, cry it through the streets.
CASSIUS. Some of you to the common pulpits, and cry out, "Liberty, freedom, and emancipation!"
BRUTUS. People and senators, don't be frightened. Don't flee — stand still. Ambition's debt is paid.
CASCA. Go to the pulpit, Brutus.
DECIUS. And Cassius too.
BRUTUS. Where's Publius?
CINNA. Here, completely bewildered by this commotion.
METELLUS. Stay close together, in case some friend of Caesar's should happen—
BRUTUS. Don't talk of standing close. Publius, take heart — no harm is intended to your person, nor to any other Roman. Tell them so, Publius.
CASSIUS. And leave us, Publius, in case the people rushing in on us should do harm to your old age.
BRUTUS. Do so — and let no man bear the blame for this deed but we who did it.
[Enter Trebonius.]
CASSIUS. Where's Antony?
TREBONIUS. Fled to his house, stunned. Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run as though it were doomsday.
BRUTUS. Fates, we will know what you please. That we shall die, we know — it's only the timing and the stretching out of days that men insist on.
CASCA. Why, he who cuts off twenty years of life cuts off so many years of fearing death.

BRUTUS. Grant that, and death becomes a benefit. So we are Caesar's friends, who've shortened his time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop, and let's bathe our hands in Caesar's blood up to the elbows and smear our swords. Then we'll walk out, all the way to the marketplace, and waving our red weapons over our heads, let's all cry, "Peace, freedom, and liberty!"
CASSIUS. Stoop then, and wash. How many ages in the future shall this lofty scene of ours be acted over, in nations not yet born and in languages not yet known!
BRUTUS. How many times shall Caesar bleed in play — Caesar who now lies stretched out at Pompey's pedestal, worth no more than the dust!
CASSIUS. As often as that happens, so often shall our band be called the men who gave their country liberty.
DECIUS. What — shall we go out?
CASSIUS. Yes, every man away. Brutus shall lead, and we'll grace his heels with the boldest and best hearts of Rome.
[Enter a Servant.]
BRUTUS. Quiet — who comes here? A friend of Antony's.

SERVANT. Thus, Brutus, did my master tell me to kneel. Thus Mark Antony told me to fall down — and prostrate, this is what he told me to say: Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest; Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving. Say that I love Brutus and honor him; say that I feared Caesar, honored him, and loved him. If Brutus will guarantee that Antony may come to him safely and be told how Caesar deserved to die, Mark Antony will not love Caesar dead as well as he'll love Brutus living, but will follow the fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus through the hazards of this untrodden state with all true faith. So says my master Antony.
BRUTUS. Your master is a wise and valiant Roman; I never thought him less. Tell him that, if he wishes to come to this place, he shall be satisfied — and, by my honor, depart untouched.
SERVANT. I'll fetch him at once.
[Exit.]
BRUTUS. I know that we shall have him as a good friend.
CASSIUS. I hope we may. But still I have a mind that fears him much — and my misgiving still falls shrewdly on target.
[Enter Antony.]
BRUTUS. But here comes Antony. Welcome, Mark Antony.

ANTONY. O mighty Caesar! Do you lie so low? Are all your conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils, shrunk to this little measure? Fare you well. I don't know, gentlemen, what you intend — who else must be bled, who else is ripe for it. If myself, there is no hour so fit as the hour of Caesar's death; no instrument of half that value as those swords of yours, made rich with the noblest blood of all this world. I beg you, if you bear a grudge against me, now, while your purple hands still reek and smoke, fulfill your pleasure. Live a thousand years, and I shall never find myself so ready to die. No place will please me so, no means of death, as here by Caesar, and cut off by you, the choice and master spirits of this age.

BRUTUS. O Antony, don't beg your death from us. Though we must now appear bloody and cruel — as our hands and this present act show we are — yet you see only our hands and the bloody business they have done. You don't see our hearts; they are pitiful. And pity for the general wrong done to Rome — as fire drives out fire, so pity drives out pity — has done this deed on Caesar. As for you, our swords have leaden points toward you, Mark Antony. Our arms, however strong in malice, and our hearts, of a brother's temper, take you in with all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.
CASSIUS. Your voice shall be as strong as any man's in the disposing of new honors.

BRUTUS. Only be patient until we've calmed the multitude, who are beside themselves with fear; then we'll explain to you the reason why I, who loved Caesar when I struck him, have done what I've done.

ANTONY. I don't doubt your wisdom. Let each man give me his bloody hand. First, Marcus Brutus, I'll shake with you. Next, Caius Cassius, I take your hand. Now, Decius Brutus, yours; now yours, Metellus; yours, Cinna; and, my valiant Casca, yours. Though last, not least in love, yours, good Trebonius. Gentlemen all — alas, what shall I say? My credit now stands on such slippery ground that you must take me for one of two bad things — either a coward or a flatterer. That I loved you, Caesar, oh, it's true. If then your spirit looks down on us now, won't it grieve you more dearly than your death to see your Antony making his peace, shaking the bloody fingers of your foes — most noble! — in the presence of your corpse? If I had as many eyes as you have wounds, weeping as fast as they stream forth your blood, it would become me better than to close in friendship with your enemies. Pardon me, Julius! Here you were brought to bay, brave hart; here you fell; and here your hunters stand, marked with your spoil and crimsoned in your stream of death. O world, you were the forest to this hart — and this indeed, O world, was the heart of you. How like a deer struck down by many princes you lie here!
CASSIUS. Mark Antony—
ANTONY. Pardon me, Caius Cassius. The enemies of Caesar will say this; coming from a friend, it's a cold modesty.
CASSIUS. I don't blame you for praising Caesar so. But what arrangement do you mean to have with us? Will you be counted among our friends, or shall we proceed, and not depend on you?

ANTONY. That's why I took your hands — but I was indeed swayed from the point by looking down on Caesar. I am friends with you all, and love you all, on this hope: that you'll give me the reasons why, and in what way, Caesar was dangerous.
BRUTUS. Otherwise this would be a savage spectacle. Our reasons are so full of sound consideration that, were you, Antony, the son of Caesar, you would be satisfied.
ANTONY. That's all I seek. And further, I'm a suitor that I may carry his body to the marketplace, and from the pulpit, as befits a friend, speak in the ceremony of his funeral.
BRUTUS. You shall, Mark Antony.
CASSIUS. Brutus, a word with you.
[Aside to Brutus.] You don't know what you're doing. Don't consent
to Antony speaking at his funeral. Do you realize how much the people may be moved by what he'll say?
BRUTUS.
[Aside to Cassius.] Forgive me —

I'll go up into the pulpit first myself and explain the reason for our Caesar's death. Whatever Antony says, I'll declare that he speaks with our leave and by our permission, and that we are content that Caesar shall have all proper rites and lawful ceremonies. It will help us more than harm us.
CASSIUS.
[Aside to Brutus.] I don't know what may happen — I don't like it.

BRUTUS. Mark Antony, here — take Caesar's body. In your funeral speech you shall not blame us, but speak all the good of Caesar you can devise, and say you do it by our permission. Otherwise, you shall have no part at all in his funeral. And you shall speak in the same pulpit I'm going to, after my speech is finished.
ANTONY. So be it. I ask for nothing more.
BRUTUS. Prepare the body then, and follow us.
[Exeunt all but Antony.]

ANTONY. Oh, pardon me, you bleeding piece of earth, that I am meek and gentle with these butchers. You are the ruins of the noblest man that ever lived in the tide of times. Woe to the hand that shed this costly blood! Over your wounds now I prophesy — wounds that, like dumb mouths, open their ruby lips to beg the voice and utterance of my tongue — a curse shall light upon the limbs of men. Domestic fury and fierce civil strife shall cumber every part of Italy. Blood and destruction shall be so common, and dreadful sights so familiar, that mothers will only smile when they see their infants cut to pieces by the hands of war. All pity will be choked with the habit of cruel deeds. And Caesar's spirit, ranging for revenge, with Ate at his side, fresh and hot from Hell, shall in this country, with a monarch's voice, cry havoc and let slip the dogs of war — so that this foul deed shall stink above the earth with bodies of the dead, groaning for burial.
[Enter a Servant.]
You serve Octavius Caesar, don't you?
SERVANT. I do, Mark Antony.
ANTONY. Caesar wrote for him to come to Rome.
SERVANT. He received his letters and is coming, and told me to say to you by word of mouth—
[Seeing the body.] O Caesar!
ANTONY. Your heart is full. Step aside and weep. Passion, I see, is catching — for my eyes, seeing those beads of sorrow stand in yours, began to water. Is your master coming?
SERVANT. He lies tonight within seven leagues of Rome.

ANTONY. Hurry back, and tell him what has happened. Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome — no Rome of safety for Octavius yet. Hurry away and tell him so. Yet stay a while — you shall not go back until I've carried this corpse to the marketplace. There I'll test, in my oration, how the people take the cruel work of these bloody men, and you can report accordingly to young Octavius on the state of things. Lend me your hand.
[Exeunt with Caesar's body.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same. The Forum
paragraphs: [Enter Brutus and goes into the pulpit, and Cassius, with a throng of Citizens.]
CITIZENS. We demand an explanation. Let us be satisfied.

BRUTUS. Then follow me, and give me your attention, friends. Cassius, go into the other street and divide the crowd. Those who want to hear me speak, let them stay here; those who want to follow Cassius, go with him. Public reasons shall be given for Caesar's death.
FIRST CITIZEN. I'll hear Brutus speak.
SECOND CITIZEN. I'll hear Cassius — and compare their reasons when I've heard them given separately.
[Exit Cassius, with some of the Citizens. Brutus goes into the rostrum.]
THIRD CITIZEN. The noble Brutus has gone up. Silence!

BRUTUS. Be patient till the end. Romans, countrymen, and friends, hear me for my cause — and be silent, so you may hear. Believe me for my honor, and have respect for my honor, so you may believe. Judge me by your own good sense, and rouse your faculties so you may judge better. If there is any in this assembly, any dear friend of Caesar's, to him I say that Brutus's love for Caesar was no less than his. If then that friend demands why Brutus rose against Caesar, this is my answer: not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more. Would you rather have Caesar living, and all die slaves, than have Caesar dead, to live all free men? As Caesar loved me, I weep for him; as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; as he was valiant, I honor him; but, as he was ambitious, I killed him. There are tears for his love; joy for his fortune; honor for his valor; and death for his ambition. Who here is so base that he would be a slave? If any, speak — for he is the one I have offended. Who here is so rude that he would not be a Roman? If any, speak — for he is the one I have offended. Who here is so vile that he won't love his country? If any, speak — for he is the one I have offended. I pause for a reply.
CITIZENS. None, Brutus, none.

BRUTUS. Then I have offended no one. I have done no more to Caesar than you shall do to Brutus. The record of his death is filed in the Capitol — his glory not understated where he was worthy of it, nor his offenses pressed beyond where he suffered death for them.
[Enter Antony and others, with Caesar's body.]

Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who, though he had no hand in his death, shall receive the benefit of his dying — a place in the commonwealth, as which of you shall not? With this I depart: that, as I killed my best lover for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger ready for myself, when my country shall need my death.
CITIZENS. Live, Brutus! Live, live!
FIRST CITIZEN. Bring him home to his house in triumph.
SECOND CITIZEN. Give him a statue alongside his ancestors.
THIRD CITIZEN. Let him be Caesar.
FOURTH CITIZEN. Caesar's better parts shall be crowned in Brutus.
FIRST CITIZEN. We'll bring him to his house with shouts and cheers.
BRUTUS. My countrymen—
SECOND CITIZEN. Quiet! Silence! Brutus speaks.
FIRST CITIZEN. Quiet there!

BRUTUS. Good countrymen, let me leave alone, and, for my sake, stay here with Antony. Do honor to Caesar's corpse, and grace his speech praising Caesar's glories, which Mark Antony, by our permission, is allowed to make. I beg you, not a man depart, except me alone, until Antony has spoken.
[Exit.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Stay! And let's hear Mark Antony.
THIRD CITIZEN. Let him go up into the public chair. We'll hear him. Noble Antony, go up.
ANTONY. For Brutus's sake, I am beholden to you.
[Goes up.]
FOURTH CITIZEN. What does he say about Brutus?
THIRD CITIZEN. He says that, for Brutus's sake, he finds himself beholden to us all.
FOURTH CITIZEN. He'd better not speak any ill of Brutus here.
FIRST CITIZEN. This Caesar was a tyrant.
THIRD CITIZEN. No question of that. We are blessed that Rome is rid of him.
SECOND CITIZEN. Quiet! Let's hear what Antony can say.
ANTONY. You gentle Romans—
CITIZENS. Quiet! Let's hear him.

ANTONY. Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears. I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. The evil that men do lives after them; the good is often buried with their bones. So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus has told you Caesar was ambitious. If it was so, it was a grievous fault, and Caesar has grievously answered for it. Here, with the permission of Brutus and the rest — for Brutus is an honorable man, and so are they all, all honorable men — I come to speak at Caesar's funeral. He was my friend, faithful and just to me; but Brutus says he was ambitious, and Brutus is an honorable man. He brought many captives home to Rome, whose ransoms filled the general coffers. Did this in Caesar seem ambitious? When the poor have cried, Caesar has wept; ambition should be made of sterner stuff. Yet Brutus says he was ambitious, and Brutus is an honorable man. You all saw that on the Lupercal I three times offered him a king's crown, which he three times refused. Was this ambition? Yet Brutus says he was ambitious, and surely he is an honorable man. I speak not to disprove what Brutus said, but here I am to speak what I know. You all loved him once, not without cause. What cause withholds you now from mourning for him? O judgment, you've fled to brutish beasts, and men have lost their reason. Bear with me. My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar, and I must pause until it comes back to me.
FIRST CITIZEN. There seems to be much sense in what he says.
SECOND CITIZEN. If you consider the matter rightly, Caesar has been done a great wrong.
THIRD CITIZEN. Has he, friends? I'm afraid a worse one will come in his place.
FOURTH CITIZEN. Did you mark his words? He wouldn't take the crown. So it's certain he wasn't ambitious.
FIRST CITIZEN. If that proves true, some will pay dearly for it.
SECOND CITIZEN. Poor soul, his eyes are red as fire from weeping.
THIRD CITIZEN. There's no nobler man in Rome than Antony.
FOURTH CITIZEN. Now watch him — he begins to speak again.

ANTONY. Only yesterday Caesar's word might have stood against the world; now he lies there, and none so poor as to do him reverence. O masters! If I were inclined to stir your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage, I would do Brutus wrong and Cassius wrong — who, as you all know, are honorable men. I will not do them wrong; I would rather wrong the dead, and wrong myself and you, than wrong such honorable men. But here's a parchment with the seal of Caesar — I found it in his study; it's his will. Just let the commons hear this testament — which, pardon me, I don't mean to read — and they would go and kiss dead Caesar's wounds, and dip their handkerchiefs in his sacred blood; yes, beg a hair from him as a keepsake, and, dying, mention it in their wills, leaving it as a rich legacy to their heirs.
FOURTH CITIZEN. We'll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony.
CITIZENS. The will, the will! We'll hear Caesar's will.

ANTONY. Be patient, gentle friends, I mustn't read it. It's not right that you should know how Caesar loved you. You're not wood, you're not stones — you're men. And being men, hearing the will of Caesar, it will inflame you, it will make you mad. It's good you don't know that you are his heirs — for if you knew, oh, what would come of it?
FOURTH CITIZEN. Read the will! We'll hear it, Antony — you shall read us the will, Caesar's will!
ANTONY. Will you be patient? Will you wait a while? I've overshot myself to mention it. I'm afraid I wrong the honorable men whose daggers have stabbed Caesar — I do fear it.
FOURTH CITIZEN. They were traitors. Honorable men!
CITIZENS. The will! The testament!
SECOND CITIZEN. They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!
ANTONY. Will you compel me, then, to read the will? Then make a ring around the corpse of Caesar, and let me show you him that made the will. Shall I come down? And will you give me leave?
CITIZENS. Come down.
SECOND CITIZEN. Descend.
[He comes down.]
THIRD CITIZEN. You shall have leave.
FOURTH CITIZEN. A ring! Stand around.
FIRST CITIZEN. Stand back from the hearse, stand back from the body.
SECOND CITIZEN. Room for Antony, most noble Antony!
ANTONY. No, don't press in on me — stand off.
CITIZENS. Stand back! Room! Move back!

ANTONY. If you have tears, prepare to shed them now. You all know this cloak. I remember the first time Caesar ever put it on; it was on a summer evening, in his tent, the day he conquered the Nervii. Look — here Cassius's dagger ran through. See what a rent the envious Casca made. Through this one the well-beloved Brutus stabbed; and as he pulled his cursed steel away, look how the blood of Caesar followed it, as if rushing out of doors to discover whether or not it was Brutus who knocked so cruelly. For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar's angel. Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar loved him. This was the most unkindest cut of all. For when the noble Caesar saw him stab, ingratitude, stronger than traitors' arms, overcame him completely. Then burst his mighty heart; and, muffling his face in his cloak, at the very base of Pompey's statue (which all the while ran with blood), great Caesar fell. Oh, what a fall was there, my countrymen! Then I, and you, and all of us fell down, while bloody treason flourished over us. Oh, now you weep — and I see you feel the impact of pity. These are gracious drops. Kind souls, what — you weep at the sight of our Caesar's robes alone, wounded? Look here — here is the man himself, mangled, as you see, by traitors.
FIRST CITIZEN. O piteous sight!
SECOND CITIZEN. O noble Caesar!
THIRD CITIZEN. O woeful day!
FOURTH CITIZEN. O traitors! Villains!
FIRST CITIZEN. O most bloody sight!
SECOND CITIZEN. We will be revenged.
CITIZENS. Revenge — search — burn — fire — kill — slay — don't let a traitor live!
ANTONY. Wait, countrymen.
FIRST CITIZEN. Quiet there! Hear the noble Antony.
SECOND CITIZEN. We'll hear him, we'll follow him, we'll die with him.

ANTONY. Good friends, sweet friends, don't let me stir you up to such a sudden flood of mutiny. Those who have done this deed are honorable. What private griefs they have, alas, I don't know, that made them do it. They are wise and honorable, and will, no doubt, give you their reasons. I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts. I am no orator, as Brutus is — but, as you all know me, a plain blunt man who loves his friend; and they know that full well who gave me public leave to speak of him. For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth, action, nor delivery, nor the power of speech to stir men's blood. I only speak plainly. I tell you what you yourselves know — show you sweet Caesar's wounds, poor poor dumb mouths, and tell them to speak for me. But if I were Brutus, and Brutus Antony, there would be an Antony to ruffle up your spirits and put a tongue in every wound of Caesar that would move the stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.
CITIZENS. We'll mutiny!
FIRST CITIZEN. We'll burn the house of Brutus.
THIRD CITIZEN. Away then! Come, find the conspirators.
ANTONY. Hear me yet, countrymen — hear me speak yet.
CITIZENS. Quiet there! Hear Antony — most noble Antony.
ANTONY. Why, friends, you go to do you know not what. How has Caesar deserved your love like this? Alas, you don't know. I must tell you then. You've forgotten the will I told you of.
CITIZENS. True enough — the will! Let's stay and hear the will.
ANTONY. Here is the will, under Caesar's seal. To every Roman citizen he gives — to every single man — seventy-five drachmas.
SECOND CITIZEN. Most noble Caesar! We'll avenge his death.
THIRD CITIZEN. O royal Caesar!
ANTONY. Hear me with patience.
CITIZENS. Quiet there!

ANTONY. Moreover, he has left you all his walks, his private gardens, and newly planted orchards, on this side of the Tiber. He has left them to you, and to your heirs forever — common pleasures, to walk abroad and recreate yourselves in. Here was a Caesar! When comes another like him?
FIRST CITIZEN. Never, never. Come, away, away! We'll burn his body in the holy place, and with those torches set fire to the traitors' houses. Take up the body.
SECOND CITIZEN. Go, fetch fire.
THIRD CITIZEN. Pull down benches.
FOURTH CITIZEN. Pull down forms, windows, anything.
[Exeunt Citizens, with the body.]
ANTONY. Now let it work. Mischief, you are afoot — take whatever course you will!
[Enter a Servant.]
How now, fellow?
SERVANT. Sir, Octavius has already come to Rome.
ANTONY. Where is he?
SERVANT. He and Lepidus are at Caesar's house.
ANTONY. And there I'll go straightaway to see him. He comes just as I wished. Fortune is in a good mood, and will give us anything we ask.
SERVANT. I heard him say Brutus and Cassius have ridden like madmen through the gates of Rome.
ANTONY. Probably they had some word of how I'd moved the people. Bring me to Octavius.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — The same. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Cinna, the poet, and after him the citizens.]
CINNA. I dreamt tonight that I feasted with Caesar, and unlucky things weigh on my imagination. I've no wish to wander outside, yet something draws me out.
FIRST CITIZEN. What's your name?
SECOND CITIZEN. Where are you going?
THIRD CITIZEN. Where do you live?
FOURTH CITIZEN. Are you married or a bachelor?
SECOND CITIZEN. Answer every man directly.
FIRST CITIZEN. Yes, and briefly.
FOURTH CITIZEN. Yes, and wisely.
THIRD CITIZEN. Yes, and truly — you'd better.
CINNA. What is my name? Where am I going? Where do I live? Am I married or a bachelor? Well — to answer every man directly and briefly, wisely and truly: wisely, I say, I am a bachelor.
SECOND CITIZEN. That's as much as to say those who marry are fools — you'll get a slap from me for that, I fear. Proceed — directly.
CINNA. Directly, I'm going to Caesar's funeral.
FIRST CITIZEN. As a friend, or an enemy?
CINNA. As a friend.
SECOND CITIZEN. That matter is answered directly.
FOURTH CITIZEN. As for where you live, briefly.
CINNA. Briefly, I live by the Capitol.
THIRD CITIZEN. Your name, sir — truly.
CINNA. Truly, my name is Cinna.
FIRST CITIZEN. Tear him to pieces! He's a conspirator.
CINNA. I'm Cinna the poet, I'm Cinna the poet.
FOURTH CITIZEN. Tear him for his bad verses, tear him for his bad verses!
CINNA. I'm not Cinna the conspirator.
FOURTH CITIZEN. It doesn't matter — his name's Cinna. Just pluck his name out of his heart and send him on his way.
THIRD CITIZEN. Tear him, tear him! Come — torches! Firebrands! To Brutus's, to Cassius's; burn it all. Some to Decius's house, and some to Casca's, some to Ligarius's. Away! Go!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Rome. A room in Antony’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus, seated at a table.]
ANTONY. These many men, then, shall die — their names are marked.
OCTAVIUS. Your brother too must die. Do you agree, Lepidus?
LEPIDUS. I agree—
OCTAVIUS. Mark him down, Antony.
LEPIDUS. — on condition that Publius shall not live, who is your sister's son, Mark Antony.
ANTONY. He shall not live. Look — with a mark I condemn him. But, Lepidus, you go to Caesar's house. Fetch the will here, and we'll determine how to cut some expense out of the legacies.
LEPIDUS. Will I find you here?
OCTAVIUS. Either here or at the Capitol.
[Exit Lepidus.]
ANTONY. This is a slight, undeserving man — fit only to be sent on errands. Is it right, with the world divided in three, that he should stand as one of the three to share it?
OCTAVIUS. So you thought of him — and took his vote on who should be marked to die in our black sentence and proscription.

ANTONY. Octavius, I've seen more days than you. And though we lay these honors on this man to free ourselves of various slanderous loads, he shall only carry them as an ass carries gold — groaning and sweating under the burden, either led or driven, as we point the way. And once he's brought our treasure where we want it, then we take his load down and turn him off, like an empty ass, to shake his ears and graze on the common.
OCTAVIUS. You can do as you wish — but he's a tried and valiant soldier.

ANTONY. So is my horse, Octavius — and for that I give him plenty of fodder. He's a creature I teach to fight, to wheel, to stop, to run straight on, his bodily motion governed by my spirit. And, in much the same way, so is Lepidus.
