He must be taught, and trained, and told to go forth — a barren-spirited fellow, one who feeds on out-of-fashion things, arts, and imitations, which, once worn out and stale to other men, begin to be his style. Don't talk of him as more than a property. And now, Octavius, listen to great things. Brutus and Cassius are raising forces — we must immediately march to meet them. So let our alliance be tightened, our best friends won over, our means stretched. And let's go sit in council now, on how secret matters may best be disclosed, and open dangers most surely answered.
OCTAVIUS. Let's do so — for we are at the stake, surrounded by many enemies. And some who smile have in their hearts, I fear, millions of mischiefs.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Before Brutus’ tent, in the camp near Sardis
paragraphs: [Drum. Enter Brutus, Lucilius, Titinius, and Soldiers; Pindarus meeting them; Lucius at some distance.]
BRUTUS. Halt!
LUCILIUS. Pass the word — halt!
BRUTUS. What now, Lucilius? Is Cassius near?
LUCILIUS. He's close by, and Pindarus has come to give you a greeting from his master.
[Pindarus gives a letter to Brutus.]

BRUTUS. He greets me well. Your master, Pindarus, whether by his own change or through bad officers, has given me good reason to wish certain done things undone. But if he's close at hand, I'll be satisfied.
PINDARUS. I have no doubt that my noble master will show himself just as he is — full of consideration and honor.
BRUTUS. He's not doubted. A word, Lucilius — tell me how he received you.
LUCILIUS. With courtesy and with enough respect, but not with the familiar manner, nor with the free and friendly conversation he used to show.

BRUTUS. You've described a hot friend cooling. Always note this, Lucilius: when love begins to sicken and decay, it resorts to forced ceremony. There are no tricks in plain and simple faith. But hollow men, like horses keen in the start, make a gallant show and promise of their mettle—
[Low march within.]
—but when they should endure the bloody spur, they drop their crests, and like deceitful nags fail in the test. Is his army coming on?
LUCILIUS. They mean to be quartered in Sardis tonight. The greater part — the cavalry as a whole — has come with Cassius.
[Enter Cassius and Soldiers.]
BRUTUS. Listen — he's arrived. March gently on to meet him.
CASSIUS. Halt!
BRUTUS. Halt! Pass the word along.
FIRST SOLDIER. Halt!
SECOND SOLDIER. Halt!
THIRD SOLDIER. Halt!
CASSIUS. Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.
BRUTUS. Judge me, you gods. Do I wrong my enemies? And if not, how could I wrong a brother?
CASSIUS. Brutus, this composed manner of yours hides wrongs — and when you do them—

BRUTUS. Cassius, be content. Speak your grievances softly. I know you well. Here, before the eyes of both our armies — which should see nothing but love between us — let's not quarrel. Tell them to move off; then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge upon your grievances, and I'll give you a hearing.
CASSIUS. Pindarus, tell our commanders to lead their men a little way off from this spot.
BRUTUS. Lucilius, do the same. And let no man come to our tent until we've finished our conference. Lucius and Titinius, guard our door.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — Within the tent of Brutus
paragraphs: [Enter Brutus and Cassius.]

CASSIUS. That you have wronged me appears in this: you've condemned and publicly noted Lucius Pella for taking bribes here from the Sardians — and in that matter my letters, pleading on his side, because I knew the man, were brushed aside.
BRUTUS. You wronged yourself to write in such a case.
CASSIUS. In a time like this, it isn't fitting that every petty offense should be commented on.
BRUTUS. Let me tell you, Cassius — you yourself are widely condemned for having an itching palm — for selling and marketing your offices for gold to undeserving men.
CASSIUS. I, an itching palm? You know that you are Brutus who speaks this — or, by the gods, that speech would otherwise have been your last.
BRUTUS. The name of Cassius lends honor to this corruption, and so punishment hides its head.
CASSIUS. Punishment!

BRUTUS. Remember March, remember the Ides of March. Did not great Julius bleed for justice's sake? What villain who stabbed his body touched him, and not for justice? What! Shall one of us, who struck down the foremost man of all this world for supporting robbers, shall we now contaminate our fingers with base bribes, and sell the mighty space of our wide honors for so much trash as can be grasped in a fist? I would rather be a dog and bay the moon than be such a Roman.
CASSIUS. Brutus, don't bait me — I won't endure it. You forget yourself by hemming me in. I am a soldier, I — older in practice, abler than yourself to make terms.
BRUTUS. Come now — you are not, Cassius.
CASSIUS. I am.
BRUTUS. I say you are not.
CASSIUS. Push me no further — I'll forget myself. Look out for your safety; tempt me no farther.
BRUTUS. Away, slight man!
CASSIUS. Is it possible?
BRUTUS. Hear me, for I will speak. Must I give way and room to your rash temper? Shall I be frightened when a madman stares?
CASSIUS. O you gods, you gods! Must I endure all this?

BRUTUS. All this? Yes, and more. Fret till your proud heart breaks. Go show your slaves how angry you are, and make your servants tremble. Must I yield? Must I take notice of you? Must I stand and crouch under your testy mood? By the gods, you shall digest the venom of your spleen, even if it splits you — for from this day forth, I'll use you for my mirth, yes, for my laughter, whenever you turn waspish.
CASSIUS. Has it come to this?
BRUTUS. You say you are a better soldier. Let it appear so. Make your boast true, and it will please me well. As for me, I shall be glad to learn from noble men.
CASSIUS. You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus. I said "an elder soldier," not "a better." Did I say better?
BRUTUS. If you did, I don't care.
CASSIUS. When Caesar lived, he wouldn't have dared to move me like this.
BRUTUS. Quiet, quiet — you wouldn't have dared to provoke him so.
CASSIUS. I would not have dared?
BRUTUS. No.
CASSIUS. What? Not dared to provoke him?
BRUTUS. For your life you would not have dared.
CASSIUS. Don't presume too much upon my love. I may do something I'll be sorry for.

BRUTUS. You have done something you should be sorry for. There's no terror, Cassius, in your threats — for I am so strongly armed in honesty that they pass by me like the idle wind, which I take no notice of. I sent to you for certain sums of gold, which you denied me — for I can raise no money by vile means. By heaven, I would rather coin my heart and drop my blood for drachmas than wring from the hard hands of peasants their vile trash by any indirection. I did send to you for gold to pay my legions, which you denied me. Was that done like Cassius? Would I have answered Caius Cassius so? When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous as to lock up such worthless coins from his friends, be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts — dash him to pieces!
CASSIUS. I did not deny you.
BRUTUS. You did.
CASSIUS. I did not. He was only a fool who brought my answer back. Brutus has split my heart. A friend should bear his friend's failings, but Brutus makes mine greater than they are.
BRUTUS. I don't — until you practice them on me.
CASSIUS. You don't love me.
BRUTUS. I don't like your faults.
CASSIUS. A friendly eye could never see such faults.
BRUTUS. A flatterer's wouldn't, even if they appeared as huge as high Olympus.

CASSIUS. Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come — revenge yourselves on Cassius alone, for Cassius is weary of the world: hated by one he loves; defied by his brother; rebuked like a slave; all his faults observed, set down in a notebook, learned and memorized by rote, to be thrown into my teeth. Oh, I could weep my spirit out of my eyes! There is my dagger, and here is my naked breast. Inside, a heart dearer than Plutus's mine, richer than gold. If you are a Roman, take it out. I, who denied you gold, will give my heart. Strike, as you struck at Caesar — for I know that when you hated him most, you loved him better than ever you loved Cassius.

BRUTUS. Sheathe your dagger. Be angry whenever you wish, it shall have free rein. Do what you will — dishonor shall be called a mood. O Cassius, you are yoked with a lamb that carries anger as flint carries fire — which, when much struck, shows a brief spark, and is immediately cold again.
CASSIUS. Has Cassius lived only to be mirth and laughter to his Brutus, when grief and a bad temper trouble him?
BRUTUS. When I spoke that, I was bad-tempered too.
CASSIUS. Do you admit so much? Give me your hand.
BRUTUS. And my heart too.
CASSIUS. O Brutus!
BRUTUS. What's the matter?
CASSIUS. Don't you have love enough to bear with me, when that rash temper my mother gave me makes me forgetful?
BRUTUS. Yes, Cassius. And from now on, when you're over-vehement with your Brutus, he'll think your mother is scolding, and leave you to it.
[Enter Poet, followed by Lucilius, Titinius, and Lucius.]
POET.
[Within.] Let me in to see the generals.
There's some grudge between them. It isn't right that they should be alone.
LUCILIUS.
[Within.] You shall not come in to them.
POET.
[Within.] Nothing but death shall stop me.
CASSIUS. What now! What's the matter?
POET. For shame, you generals! What do you mean? Love, and be friends, as two such men should be — for I have seen more years, I'm sure, than you.
CASSIUS. Ha, ha! How vilely this cynic rhymes!
BRUTUS. Get out of here, fellow. Cheeky man, away!
CASSIUS. Bear with him, Brutus — it's his way.
BRUTUS. I'll bear his manner when he learns his timing. What should the wars do with these jingling fools? Companion, away!
CASSIUS. Away, away, be gone!
[Exit Poet.]
BRUTUS. Lucilius and Titinius, tell the commanders to prepare to lodge their companies tonight.
CASSIUS. And come yourselves back, and bring Messala with you immediately to us.
[Exeunt Lucilius and Titinius.]
BRUTUS. Lucius, a bowl of wine.
[Exit Lucius.]
CASSIUS. I didn't think you could have been so angry.
BRUTUS. O Cassius, I am sick with many griefs.
CASSIUS. You make no use of your philosophy, if you yield to accidental evils.
BRUTUS. No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.
CASSIUS. Ha? Portia?
BRUTUS. She is dead.
CASSIUS. How did I escape being killed, when I crossed you so? O insupportable and touching loss! Of what illness?

BRUTUS. Impatient at my absence, and grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony have made themselves so strong — for with her death the news of that came. With this she fell distracted, and, her attendants absent, swallowed fire.
CASSIUS. And died that way?
BRUTUS. Just so.
CASSIUS. O you immortal gods!
[Enter Lucius, with wine and a taper.]
BRUTUS. Speak no more of her. Give me a bowl of wine. In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.
[Drinks.]
CASSIUS. My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge. Fill, Lucius, till the wine overflows the cup. I cannot drink too much of Brutus's love.
[Drinks.]
[Exit Lucius.]
[Enter Titinius and Messala.]
BRUTUS. Come in, Titinius! Welcome, good Messala. Now let's sit close around this candle here, and consider what we need to do.
CASSIUS. Portia, are you gone?
BRUTUS. No more, I beg you. Messala, I've received letters here that young Octavius and Mark Antony are coming down on us with a mighty force, directing their expedition toward Philippi.
MESSALA. I myself have letters with the same content.
BRUTUS. With what addition?
MESSALA. That by proscription and bills of outlawry Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus have put to death a hundred senators.
BRUTUS. In that, our letters don't quite agree. Mine speak of seventy senators who died by their proscriptions — Cicero being one.
CASSIUS. Cicero, one?
MESSALA. Cicero is dead, by that order of proscription. Did you get your letters from your wife, my lord?
BRUTUS. No, Messala.
MESSALA. Nothing in your letters written about her?
BRUTUS. Nothing, Messala.
MESSALA. That, it seems to me, is strange.
BRUTUS. Why do you ask? Did you hear anything of her in yours?
MESSALA. No, my lord.
BRUTUS. Now as you are a Roman, tell me the truth.
MESSALA. Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell — for certainly she is dead, and by a strange manner.
BRUTUS. Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala. Through meditating that she must die at some point, I have the patience to endure it now.
MESSALA. Just so great men should endure great losses.
CASSIUS. I have as much of this resolve in principle as you do — yet my nature couldn't bear it so.
BRUTUS. Well, to our living work. What do you think of marching to Philippi right away?
CASSIUS. I don't think it good.
BRUTUS. Your reason?
CASSIUS. This: it's better that the enemy seek us out. That way he wastes his means, tires his soldiers, doing himself harm — while we, lying still, are full of rest, defense, and nimbleness.

BRUTUS. Good reasons must necessarily give place to better ones. The people between Philippi and this ground stand with us only by a forced affection — they've grudged us their contribution. The enemy, marching past them, will gather them up to swell his numbers, and come on refreshed, newly added to, and encouraged. From which advantage we shall cut him off if at Philippi we face him there, with these people at our back.
CASSIUS. Hear me, good brother.

BRUTUS. Pardon me. You must note besides that we've tried the utmost of our friends, our legions are brimful, our cause is ripe. The enemy increases every day; we, at our peak, are ready to decline. There is a tide in the affairs of men which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; missed, all the voyage of their life is bound in shallows and in miseries. On such a full sea we are now afloat, and we must take the current when it serves, or lose our ventures.
CASSIUS. Then, by your will, go on. We'll go along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.
BRUTUS. The depth of night has crept upon our talk, and nature must obey necessity, which we will treat stingily with a little rest. Is there anything more to say?
CASSIUS. No more. Good night. Early tomorrow we'll rise, and away.
[Enter Lucius.]
BRUTUS. Lucius! My gown.
[Exit Lucius.]
Farewell now, good Messala. Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius — good night, and good rest.
CASSIUS. O my dear brother! This was an ill beginning of the night. May such division never come between our souls again. Don't let it, Brutus.
[Enter Lucius with the gown.]
BRUTUS. Everything is well.
CASSIUS. Good night, my lord.
BRUTUS. Good night, good brother.
TITINIUS and MESSALA. Good night, Lord Brutus.
BRUTUS. Farewell, everyone.
[Exeunt Cassius, Titinius, and Messala.]
Give me the gown. Where is your instrument?
LUCIUS. Here in the tent.
BRUTUS. What, you speak drowsily? Poor knave, I don't blame you — you've been kept up too long. Call Claudius and some others of my men. I'll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.
LUCIUS. Varro and Claudius!
[Enter Varro and Claudius.]
VARRO. My lord calls?
BRUTUS. Please, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep. It may be that I'll wake you presently for business with my brother Cassius.
VARRO. If you please, we'll stand and wait on your pleasure.
BRUTUS. I won't have it so — lie down, good sirs. It may be I'll think otherwise. Look, Lucius — here's the book I was hunting for so long. I put it in the pocket of my gown.
[Servants lie down.]
LUCIUS. I was sure your lordship hadn't given it to me.
BRUTUS. Bear with me, good boy — I am very forgetful. Can you hold up your heavy eyes a while, and play a tune or two on your instrument?
LUCIUS. Yes, my lord, if it please you.
BRUTUS. It does, my boy. I trouble you too much, but you're willing.
LUCIUS. It's my duty, sir.
BRUTUS. I shouldn't press your duty beyond your strength. I know young blood looks for a time of rest.
LUCIUS. I've slept already, my lord.
BRUTUS. It was well done, and you shall sleep again. I won't keep you long. If I live, I'll be good to you.
[Lucius plays and sings till he falls asleep.]

This is a sleepy tune. O murderous slumber, do you lay your leaden mace upon my boy, who is playing you music? Gentle knave, good night — I won't do you so much wrong as to wake you. If you nod, you'll break your instrument. I'll take it from you; and, good boy, good night. Let me see, let me see — isn't the page turned down where I left off reading? Here it is, I think.
[Enter the Ghost of Caesar.]

How dimly this candle burns! Ha! Who comes here? I think it's the weakness of my eyes that shapes this monstrous apparition. It comes toward me. Are you anything? Are you some god, some angel, or some devil, that makes my blood cold and my hair stand on end? Speak to me — say what you are.
GHOST. Your evil spirit, Brutus.
BRUTUS. Why do you come?
GHOST. To tell you that you shall see me at Philippi.
BRUTUS. Well — then I shall see you again?
GHOST. Yes, at Philippi.
BRUTUS. Why, I'll see you at Philippi then.
[Ghost vanishes.]
Now I've taken heart, you vanish. Evil spirit, I would speak with you more. Boy! Lucius! Varro! Claudius! Sirs, awake! Claudius!
LUCIUS. The strings, my lord, are false.
BRUTUS. He thinks he's still at his instrument. Lucius, awake!
LUCIUS. My lord?
BRUTUS. Did you dream, Lucius, that you cried out so?
LUCIUS. My lord, I don't know that I cried out.
BRUTUS. Yes, you did. Did you see anything?
LUCIUS. Nothing, my lord.
BRUTUS. Sleep again, Lucius. Sirrah Claudius! Fellow, you — awake!
VARRO. My lord?
CLAUDIUS. My lord?
BRUTUS. Why did you both cry out, sirs, in your sleep?
VARRO. CLAUDIUS. Did we, my lord?
BRUTUS. Yes. Did you see anything?
VARRO. No, my lord, I saw nothing.
CLAUDIUS. Nor I, my lord.
BRUTUS. Go and give my regards to my brother Cassius. Tell him to set his forces moving early, ahead of us, and we will follow.
VARRO. CLAUDIUS. It shall be done, my lord.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — The plains of Philippi
paragraphs: [Enter Octavius, Antony, and their Army.]

OCTAVIUS. Now, Antony, our hopes are answered. You said the enemy wouldn't come down, but would keep to the hills and upper ground. It hasn't proved so. Their battle lines are at hand; they mean to engage us here at Philippi, answering us before we even challenge them.

ANTONY. Tut — I know what's in their hearts, and I know why they do it. They'd be content to visit other places, and come down with this fearful show of bravado, thinking by this front to make us believe they have courage. But it isn't so.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. Prepare, generals. The enemy is coming on in gallant display. Their bloody battle-flag is hung out, and something must be done at once.
ANTONY. Octavius, lead your wing gently on the left side of the level field.
OCTAVIUS. I'll take the right. You take the left.
ANTONY. Why do you cross me at this crisis?
OCTAVIUS. I'm not crossing you, but that's what I'll do.
[March.]
[Drum. Enter Brutus, Cassius, and their Army; Lucilius, Titinius, Messala, and others.]
BRUTUS. They've stopped — they want to parley.
CASSIUS. Stand fast, Titinius. We must go out and talk.
OCTAVIUS. Mark Antony, shall we give the sign for battle?
ANTONY. No, Caesar — we'll answer when they charge. Step forward; the generals want a word.
OCTAVIUS. Don't move until the signal.
BRUTUS. Words before blows — is that the way, countrymen?
OCTAVIUS. Not that we love words better, as you do.
BRUTUS. Good words are better than bad blows, Octavius.
ANTONY. In your bad blows, Brutus, you give good words — witness the hole you made in Caesar's heart while crying, "Long live! Hail, Caesar!"
CASSIUS. Antony, the quality of your blows is yet unknown — but as for your words, they rob the bees of Hybla and leave them honeyless.
ANTONY. Not stingless too?
BRUTUS. Oh yes, and soundless too — for you have stolen their buzzing, Antony, and very wisely threaten before you sting.

ANTONY. Villains, you didn't do that when your vile daggers hacked one another in Caesar's sides. You showed your teeth like apes, fawned like hounds, and bowed like slaves, kissing Caesar's feet — while damned Casca, like a cur, behind, struck Caesar on the neck. Oh, you flatterers!
CASSIUS. Flatterers! Now, Brutus, thank yourself for this. This tongue would not have offended so today, if Cassius's counsel had ruled.

OCTAVIUS. Come, come, get to the point. If arguing makes us sweat, the proof of it will turn into redder drops. Look — I draw a sword against conspirators. When do you think this sword goes back into its sheath? Never, till Caesar's three-and-thirty wounds are well avenged; or till another Caesar has added more slaughter to the sword of traitors.
BRUTUS. Caesar, you cannot die by traitors' hands, unless you bring them with you.
OCTAVIUS. So I hope. I was not born to die on Brutus's sword.
BRUTUS. Oh, if you were the noblest of your line, young man, you couldn't die more honorably.
CASSIUS. A peevish schoolboy, unworthy of such honor, joined with a masquer and a reveller.
ANTONY. Old Cassius still!
OCTAVIUS. Come, Antony — away! Traitors, we hurl defiance in your teeth. If you dare fight today, come to the field; if not, when you have the stomach for it.
[Exeunt Octavius, Antony, and their Army.]
CASSIUS. Why now, blow wind, swell billow, and swim, ship! The storm is up, and all is on the hazard.
BRUTUS. Hey, Lucilius! Listen, a word with you.
LUCILIUS. My lord?
[Brutus and Lucilius talk apart.]
CASSIUS. Messala.
MESSALA. What does my general say?

CASSIUS. Messala, this is my birthday — on this very day was Cassius born. Give me your hand, Messala. Be my witness that against my will (as it was with Pompey) I am being forced to stake all our liberties on one battle. You know I held Epicurus strongly, and his opinion. Now I change my mind, and partly credit things that foretell the future. Coming from Sardis, on our foremost standard two mighty eagles fell and there they perched, gorging and feeding from our soldiers' hands — who accompanied us here to Philippi. This morning they've flown away and gone, and in their place ravens, crows, and kites fly over our heads and look down on us as if we were sickly prey. Their shadows seem a most fatal canopy under which our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.
MESSALA. Don't believe so.
CASSIUS. I believe it only partly — for I am fresh of spirit, and resolved to meet all perils very steadily.
BRUTUS. Just so, Lucilius.

CASSIUS. Now, most noble Brutus, may the gods stand friendly to us today, so that we may, lovers in peace, live on into old age. But since the affairs of men remain ever uncertain, let's reason about the worst that may happen. If we lose this battle, then this is the very last time we shall speak together. What, then, are you determined to do?

BRUTUS. By the same principle of that philosophy by which I blamed Cato for the death he gave himself — I don't know how, but I find it cowardly and vile, for fear of what might happen, to cut short the time of life — arming myself with patience to wait on the providence of some high powers that govern us below.
CASSIUS. Then, if we lose this battle, you're content to be led in triumph through the streets of Rome?

BRUTUS. No, Cassius, no. Don't think, you noble Roman, that Brutus will ever go bound to Rome — he bears too great a mind. But this same day must end the work the Ides of March began. And whether we shall meet again I do not know. So let's take our everlasting farewell. Forever, and forever, farewell, Cassius. If we do meet again, why, we'll smile. If not, why then, this parting was well made.
CASSIUS. Forever and forever farewell, Brutus. If we do meet again, we'll smile indeed; if not, it's true this parting was well made.
BRUTUS. Why then, lead on. Oh, if a man could only know the end of this day's business before it comes! But it's enough that the day will end, and then the end is known. Come, ho! Away!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — The same. The field of battle
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter Brutus and Messala.]
BRUTUS. Ride, ride, Messala, ride — and deliver these orders to the legions on the other side.
[Loud alarum.]
Let them attack at once. I see only a cold demeanor in Octavius's wing, and a sudden push will overthrow them. Ride, ride, Messala. Let them all come down.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter Cassius and Titinius.]
CASSIUS. Oh, look, Titinius, look — the villains are running! I've turned enemy to my own side. This ensign of mine was turning back; I killed the coward and took the standard from him.
TITINIUS. O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early. Having some advantage over Octavius, he took it too eagerly. His soldiers fell to looting, while we are completely surrounded by Antony.
[Enter Pindarus.]
PINDARUS. Fly further off, my lord, fly further off. Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord. So fly, noble Cassius, fly far off.
CASSIUS. This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius — are those my tents where I see the fire?
TITINIUS. They are, my lord.

CASSIUS. Titinius, if you love me, mount my horse and dig your spurs into him, till he's brought you up to those troops over there and back here again — so that I may be sure whether those troops are friend or enemy.
TITINIUS. I'll be here again, as quick as thought.
[Exit.]
CASSIUS. Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill. My sight was always dim. Watch Titinius, and tell me what you see across the field.
[Pindarus goes up.]
This day I first breathed. Time has come full circle, and where I began, there I shall end. My life has run its course. Sirrah, what news?
PINDARUS.
[Above.] O my lord!
CASSIUS. What news?
PINDARUS.
[Above.] Titinius is surrounded
by horsemen, who are spurring toward him — yet he spurs on. Now they're almost on him. Now, Titinius! Now some dismount. Oh, he dismounts too. He's taken!
[Shout.]
And listen — they shout for joy.
CASSIUS. Come down; look no more. Oh, coward that I am, to have lived so long — to see my best friend taken before my face!
[Pindarus descends.]

Come here, sirrah. In Parthia I took you prisoner. And then I made you swear, when I saved your life, that whatever I bid you do, you'd attempt it. Now come, keep your oath. Now be a freeman; and with this good sword, that ran through Caesar's bowels, search this chest. Don't stand to answer. Here, take the hilt — and when my face is covered, as it is now, guide the sword. Caesar, you are revenged — by the very sword that killed you.
[Dies.]
PINDARUS. So I am free — yet I would not have been so, if I dared to do my will. O Cassius! Far from this country Pindarus shall run, where no Roman shall ever notice him.
[Exit.]
[Enter Titinius with Messala.]
MESSALA. It's only an exchange, Titinius. Octavius is overthrown by noble Brutus's force, just as Cassius's legions are by Antony.
TITINIUS. This news would comfort Cassius greatly.
MESSALA. Where did you leave him?
TITINIUS. All disconsolate, with Pindarus his servant, on this hill.
MESSALA. Isn't that him lying on the ground?
TITINIUS. He doesn't lie like the living. Oh my heart!
MESSALA. Isn't that him?

TITINIUS. No, this was him, Messala — but Cassius is no more. O setting sun, as in your red rays you sink toward night, so in his red blood Cassius's day is set. The sun of Rome is set. Our day is gone; clouds, dews, and dangers come; our deeds are done. Mistrust of my success has done this deed.

MESSALA. Mistrust of a good outcome has done this deed. O hateful Error, child of Melancholy! Why do you show to the receptive thoughts of men the things that are not? O Error, conceived so quickly, you never come to a happy birth, but kill the mother who engendered you.
TITINIUS. What, Pindarus! Where are you, Pindarus?

MESSALA. Look for him, Titinius, while I go to meet the noble Brutus, thrusting this report into his ears. I may well say thrusting — for piercing steel and poisoned darts will be as welcome to Brutus's ears as the news of this sight.
TITINIUS. Hurry, Messala — and I will look for Pindarus in the meantime.
[Exit Messala.]

Why did you send me out, brave Cassius? Didn't I meet your friends? And didn't they put this wreath of victory on my brows, and tell me to give it to you? Didn't you hear their shouts? Alas, you've misconstrued everything! But hold — take this garland on your brow. Your Brutus told me to give it to you, and I will do his bidding. Brutus, come quickly, and see how I honored Caius Cassius. By your leave, gods — this is a Roman's part. Come, Cassius's sword, and find Titinius's heart.
[Dies.]
[Alarum. Enter Brutus, Messala, young Cato, Strato, Volumnius, and Lucilius.]
BRUTUS. Where, where, Messala, does his body lie?
MESSALA. There, and Titinius mourning over it.
BRUTUS. Titinius's face is upward.
CATO. He's killed.
BRUTUS. O Julius Caesar, you are mighty yet! Your spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords into our own entrails.
[Low alarums.]
CATO. Brave Titinius! Look — he has crowned dead Cassius.

BRUTUS. Are any two Romans still living such as these? Last of all the Romans, fare you well. It's impossible that Rome should ever breed your equal. Friends, I owe more tears to this dead man than you shall see me pay. I shall find time, Cassius — I shall find time. Come, then, and send his body to Thassos. His funeral shall not be in our camp, lest it dishearten us. Lucilius, come — and come, young Cato. Let's to the field. Labeo and Flavius, set our battle-lines moving. It's three o'clock — and Romans, yet before night we shall try fortune in a second fight.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter fighting soldiers of both armies; then Brutus, Messala, young Cato, Lucilius, Flavius, and others.]
BRUTUS. Yet, countrymen — oh, yet hold up your heads!
CATO. What bastard doesn't? Who will go with me? I'll proclaim my name about the field. I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho! A foe to tyrants, and my country's friend. I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
[Charges the enemy.]
LUCILIUS. And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I! Brutus, my country's friend; know me for Brutus!
[Exit, charging the enemy. Cato is overpowered, and falls.]
LUCILIUS. O young and noble Cato, are you down? Why, now you die as bravely as Titinius, and may be honored, being Cato's son.
FIRST SOLDIER. Yield, or you die.
LUCILIUS. I yield only to die. There is so much here that you'll kill me straightaway.
[Offering money.]
Kill Brutus, and be honored in his death.
FIRST SOLDIER. We must not. A noble prisoner!
SECOND SOLDIER. Make way! Tell Antony, Brutus is taken.
FIRST SOLDIER. I'll bring the news. Here comes the general.
[Enter Antony.]
Brutus is taken, Brutus is taken, my lord.
ANTONY. Where is he?

LUCILIUS. Safe, Antony — Brutus is safe enough. I dare assure you that no enemy shall ever take noble Brutus alive. The gods defend him from so great a shame! When you find him, alive or dead, he will be found like Brutus, like himself.

ANTONY. This is not Brutus, friend — but, I assure you, a prize no less in worth. Keep this man safe; treat him with all kindness. I'd rather have such men as my friends than as enemies. Go on, and see whether Brutus is alive or dead, and bring us word at Octavius's tent how everything has turned out.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: [Enter Brutus, Dardanius, Clitus, Strato, and Volumnius.]
BRUTUS. Come, poor remnant of friends, rest on this rock.
CLITUS. Statilius showed the torchlight signal — but, my lord, he hasn't come back. He's either taken or killed.
BRUTUS. Sit down, Clitus. Killing is the word — it's a deed in fashion. Listen, Clitus.
[Whispering.]
CLITUS. What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.
BRUTUS. Quiet then, no words.
CLITUS. I'd rather kill myself.
BRUTUS. Listen, Dardanius.
[Whispers him.]
DARDANIUS. Should I do such a deed?
CLITUS. O Dardanius!
DARDANIUS. O Clitus!
CLITUS. What ill request did Brutus make of you?
DARDANIUS. To kill him, Clitus. Look — he's brooding.
CLITUS. Now that noble vessel is so full of grief it overflows even at his eyes.
BRUTUS. Come here, good Volumnius. Listen, a word.
VOLUMNIUS. What does my lord say?
BRUTUS. Why, this, Volumnius: the ghost of Caesar has appeared to me twice at night — at Sardis once, and this last night here on the fields of Philippi. I know my hour has come.
VOLUMNIUS. Not so, my lord.
BRUTUS. No, I'm sure it is, Volumnius. You see, Volumnius, the way the world goes — our enemies have beaten us to the pit.
[Low alarums.]

It's more worthy to leap in ourselves than to wait till they push us in. Good Volumnius, you know we two went to school together. For that long-ago love, I beg you, hold my sword-hilts while I run on it.
VOLUMNIUS. That's not an office for a friend, my lord.
[Alarums still.]
CLITUS. Fly, fly, my lord! There's no staying here.

BRUTUS. Farewell to you; and you; and you, Volumnius. Strato, you've been asleep all this while; farewell to you too, Strato. Countrymen, my heart rejoices that in all my life I found no man but was true to me. I shall have more glory by this losing day than Octavius and Mark Antony shall attain by this vile conquest. So fare you well at once; for Brutus's tongue has nearly ended his life's history. Night hangs upon my eyes. My bones would rest, that have only labored to attain this hour.
[Alarums. Cry within, "Fly, fly, fly!"]
CLITUS. Fly, my lord, fly!
BRUTUS. Away! I'll follow.
[Exeunt Clitus, Dardanius, and Volumnius.]

I beg you, Strato, stay by your lord. You are a fellow of good reputation; your life has had some touch of honor in it. Hold my sword then, and turn away your face, while I run on it. Will you, Strato?
STRATO. Give me your hand first. Fare you well, my lord.
BRUTUS. Farewell, good Strato. Caesar, now be still — I killed you not with half so good a will.
[He runs on his sword, and dies.]
[Alarum. Retreat. Enter Antony, Octavius, Messala, Lucilius, and the Army.]
OCTAVIUS. What man is that?
MESSALA. My master's man. Strato, where is your master?
STRATO. Free from the bondage you are in, Messala. The conquerors can only make a fire of him — for Brutus alone overcame himself, and no other man has honor by his death.
LUCILIUS. So Brutus should be found. I thank you, Brutus, that you have proved Lucilius's word true.
OCTAVIUS. All who served Brutus, I will take into my service. Fellow, will you spend your time with me?
STRATO. Yes, if Messala will recommend me to you.
OCTAVIUS. Do so, good Messala.
MESSALA. How did my master die, Strato?
STRATO. I held the sword, and he ran upon it.
MESSALA. Octavius, then take into your service the one who did the last service to my master.

ANTONY. This was the noblest Roman of them all. All the conspirators, except only him, did what they did out of envy of great Caesar. He alone, in a general honest thought and common good to all, made one of them. His life was gentle, and the elements so mixed in him that Nature might stand up and say to all the world, "This was a man!"

OCTAVIUS. According to his virtue, let us treat him with all respect and rites of burial. Within my tent his bones shall lie tonight, like a soldier, in honorable order. So call the field to rest, and let's away, to share the glories of this happy day.
[Exeunt.]
